14: # Skill Asset File Templates - Creation Guidelines
15: 
16: Templates and guidelines for creating asset files in AI agent skills.
17: 
18: ## 1. OVERVIEW
19: 
20: ### Location & Naming
21: 
22: **Location:** `.skilled/skills/[skill-name]/assets/`
23: 
24: **Naming Convention:** kebab-case with the appropriate extension
25: 
26: | ✅ Valid Names | ❌ Invalid Names |
27: |---------------|-----------------|
28: | `frontmatter-templates.md` | `FrontmatterTemplates.md` (PascalCase) |
29: | `config-examples.yaml` | `config_examples.yaml` (snake_case) |
30: | `validation-checklist.md` | `ValidationChecklist.MD` (wrong case) |
31: | `emoji-reference.md` | `emojiReference.md` (camelCase) |
32: 
33: ### When to Create Assets
34: 
35: **Create an asset file when:**
36: - Templates users apply repeatedly
37: - Reference data >50 lines and self-contained
38: - Multiple examples of same pattern exist
39: - Lookup tables or decision matrices needed
40: - Template variations for different scenarios
41: 
42: **Keep in SKILL.md when:**
43: - Content <30 lines
44: - Tightly coupled to workflow logic
45: - Needs to be visible immediately (not progressive disclosure)
46: - Part of core instructions (RULES, WORKFLOW sections)
47: 
48: ---
49: 
50: ## 2. ASSET FILE TYPES
51: 
52: ### Template Files
53: **Purpose**: Provide copy-paste starting points for common tasks
54: 
55: **Naming**: `[content-type]-templates.md`
56: - Example: `frontmatter-templates.md`, `structure-templates.md`
57: 
58: **Structure**:
59: - One template per section
60: - Include field descriptions
61: - Show complete examples
62: - Explain when to use each template
63: 
64: **Use cases**:
65: - Document templates (SKILL.md, commands, knowledge files)
66: - Configuration templates (YAML, JSON)
67: - Code templates (functions, classes, modules)
68: 
69: ### Reference Files
70: **Purpose**: Provide lookup tables, decision trees, or reference data
71: 
72: **Naming**: `[topic]-reference.md`
73: - Example: `emoji-reference.md`, `validation-reference.md`
74: 
75: **Structure**:
76: - Tables or lists for quick lookup
77: - Decision matrices
78: - Classification systems
79: - Standards and conventions
80: 
81: **Use cases**:
82: - Emoji selection guides
83: - File type classifications
84: - Validation rule sets
85: - Naming conventions
86: 
87: ### Example Files
88: **Purpose**: Show working examples of skill outputs
89: 
90: **Naming**: `[topic]-examples.md`
91: - Example: `optimization-examples.md`, `skill-examples.md`
92: 
93: **Structure**:
94: - Before/after comparisons
95: - Annotated examples
96: - Multiple variations
97: - Anti-patterns to avoid
98: 
99: **Use cases**:
100: - Complete skill applications
101: - Common patterns
102: - Edge cases
103: - Quality standards
104: 
105: ### Guide Files
106: **Purpose**: Detailed how-to guides for complex processes
107: 
108: **Naming**: `[process]-guide.md`
109: - Example: `packaging-guide.md`, `distribution-guide.md`
110: 
111: **Structure**:
112: - Step-by-step instructions
113: - Troubleshooting sections
114: - Best practices
115: - Common pitfalls
116: 
117: **Use cases**:
118: - Multi-step processes
119: - Advanced techniques
120: - Workflow deep-dives
121: - Integration guides
122: 
123: ---
124:

126: 
127: ### Title and Intro
128: 
129: **CRITICAL: The intro after the H1 title must be 1-2 SHORT sentences only.**

132: ---
133: title: [Title]
134: description: [One-line description - same as intro]

170: ```
171: 
172: Every asset file carries this full 5-field frontmatter block: the Skill Advisor harvests it as routing signal (3-8 lowercase multi-word `trigger_phrases` drawn from the doc's content, `importance_tier` defaults to `normal`, and `contextType` is one of `planning|research|implementation|general`). See [frontmatter-templates.md](../../../sk-create-frontmatter/assets/frontmatter-templates.md) for field rules.
173: 
174: > **WARNING: DO NOT duplicate content between intro and OVERVIEW section.**
175: > The intro is a hook. OVERVIEW provides the details.
176: 
177: #### GOOD Intro Structure
178: 
179: ```markdown
180: # Git Commit Templates
181: 
182: Copy the template that matches the change, fill the fields, and commit.
183: 
184: \## 1. OVERVIEW
185: 
186: ### Purpose
187: 
188: Uniform messages let a reader scan history by intent instead of by author.
189: 
190: ### Usage
191: 
192: Copy the appropriate template based on commit type...
193: 
194: ---
195: 
196: \## 2. COMMIT TEMPLATES
197: ...
198: ```
199: 
200: #### BAD Intro Structure (too long, has subsections)
201: 
202: ```markdown
203: # Git Commit Templates
204: 
205: Copy-paste templates for creating well-structured commit messages.
206: 
207: ### Core Principle    ← WRONG: No headers in intro!
208: Atomic commits with clear intent = maintainable history.
209: 
210: ### When to Use       ← WRONG: This belongs in OVERVIEW section!
211: - Creating new features
212: - Fixing bugs
213: 
214: ---
215: ```
216: 
217: ### Intro vs OVERVIEW Content Placement
218: 
219: | Content Type          | Intro (after H1) | OVERVIEW Section       |
220: | --------------------- | ---------------- | ---------------------- |
221: | 1-2 sentence summary  | ✅ YES            | ❌ NO (don't repeat)    |
222: | Core Principle        | ❌ NO             | ✅ YES (in Purpose)     |
223: | When to Use           | ❌ NO             | ✅ YES (in Purpose)     |
224: | How to copy/customize | ❌ NO             | ✅ YES (in Usage)       |
225: | Prerequisites         | ❌ NO             | ✅ YES (in Usage)       |
226: | Any H2/H3 subsections | ❌ NEVER          | ✅ YES                  |

305: ## 5. LOGIC REPRESENTATION PATTERNS
306: 
307: **Purpose**: Guidelines for representing logic, workflows, and decision trees in asset files using structured formats instead of prose.
308: 
309: **Why Structured Logic?**
310: - **Clarity**: Executable-style logic is easier to understand than prose
311: - **AI-Friendly**: LLMs parse structured logic better than narrative descriptions
312: - **Maintainability**: Changes to logic are more visible in structured formats
313: - **Consistency**: Same patterns across all asset files
314: 
315: ### When to Use Each Format
316: 
317: **Use Python Pseudo-Code When:**
318: - Complex branching logic (multiple IF/ELIF/ELSE conditions)
319: - Function/method definitions with clear inputs/outputs
320: - State management or algorithmic processes
321: - Validation or transformation logic
322: - Examples: Mode detection, validation pipelines, decision functions
323: 
324: **Use YAML Structures When:**
325: - Configuration data (settings, options, parameters)
326: - Pipeline definitions (multi-step workflows with clear phases)
327: - Hierarchical workflows (nested processes)
328: - Metadata structures (categorization, tagging)
329: - Examples: Workflow definitions, configuration templates, feature matrices
330: 
331: **Use Markdown Decision Trees When:**
332: - Simple branching logic (2-5 branches)
333: - Visual flow representation (user-facing paths)
334: - Classification systems (type determination)
335: - Quick decision guides
336: - Examples: Document type selection, frontmatter requirements
337: 
338: **Keep Markdown Prose When:**
339: - Explanatory text and conceptual overviews
340: - Narrative examples with context
341: - Best practices guidance
342: - Introductions and summaries
343:

346: ## 6. DECISION LOGIC EXAMPLES
347: 
348: **Purpose**: Demonstrate how to convert markdown prose into structured decision logic.
349: 
350: ### Python Pseudo-Code: Mode Detection
351: 
352: **Before (Markdown Prose)**:
353: ```markdown
354: Check user input for mode indicators:
355: - If "$quick" is present, use quick mode with auto-scaling depth
356: - If "$ticket" is present, use ticket mode with depth 10
357: - Otherwise, use interactive mode with depth 10
358: ```
359: 
360: **After (Python Pseudo-Code)**:
361: ```python
362: def detect_mode(request):
363:     """Detect execution mode from user request markers"""
364: 
365:     if '$quick' in request:
366:         mode = 'quick'
367:         depth = 'auto_scale_1_to_5'
368:     elif '$ticket' in request:
369:         mode = 'ticket'
370:         depth = 'depth_10_rounds'
371:     else:
372:         # DEFAULT TO INTERACTIVE
373:         mode = 'interactive'
374:         depth = 'depth_10_rounds'
375: 
376:     return mode, depth
377: ```
378: 
379: ### Markdown Decision Tree: Frontmatter Requirements
380: 
381: **Before (Markdown Prose)**:
382: ```markdown
383: Different document types have different frontmatter requirements:
384: - SKILL.md files must have frontmatter with name, description, allowed-tools, and version
385: - Command files must have frontmatter with description and argument-hint
386: - Skill reference/asset files must have the 5-field block
387: - Knowledge files outside skill folders should not have frontmatter
388: - Spec files typically don't have frontmatter
389: ```
390: 
391: **After (Markdown Decision Tree)**:
392: ```
393: Document type?
394: ├─> SKILL.md             → MUST have frontmatter (name, description, allowed-tools, version)
395: ├─> Command              → MUST have frontmatter (description, argument-hint, allowed-tools)
396: ├─> Skill Reference/Asset → MUST have the 5-field block (title, description,
397: │                           trigger_phrases, importance_tier, contextType)
398: ├─> Knowledge (outside skills) → MUST NOT have frontmatter (remove if present)
399: ├─> Spec                 → SHOULD NOT have frontmatter (suggest removal)
400: └─> README               → No specific requirement (usually none)
401: ```
402: 
403: ### Python Pseudo-Code: Validation Logic
404: 
405: **Before (Markdown Prose)**:
406: ```markdown
407: Validate the document structure:
408: 1. Check if required sections exist
409: 2. Verify section ordering is correct
410: 3. Ensure frontmatter is valid (if present)
411: ```
412: 
413: **After (Python Pseudo-Code)**:
414: ```python
415: def validate_document(doc, doc_type):
416:     """Validate document structure and content"""
417: 
418:     errors = []
419: 
420:     # Check required sections
421:     required_sections = get_required_sections(doc_type)
422:     for section in required_sections:
423:         if section not in doc.sections:
424:             errors.append(f"Missing required section: {section}")
425: 
426:     # Verify section ordering
427:     expected_order = get_section_order(doc_type)
428:     actual_order = [s.name for s in doc.sections]
429:     if actual_order != expected_order:
430:         errors.append(f"Section order incorrect. Expected: {expected_order}")
431: 
432:     # Validate frontmatter
433:     if doc.has_frontmatter:
434:         frontmatter_errors = validate_frontmatter(doc.frontmatter, doc_type)
435:         errors.extend(frontmatter_errors)
436: 
437:     return errors
438: ```

442: ## 7. WORKFLOW PATTERNS
443: 
444: **Purpose**: Show how to represent multi-step workflows using YAML structures.
445: 
446: ### YAML Pipeline: Document Creation Workflow
447: 
448: **Before (Markdown List)**:
449: ```markdown
450: 1. Analyze the request and determine document type
451: 2. Select appropriate template
452: 3. Populate template with content
453: 4. Validate structure and content
454: 5. Apply formatting standards
455: 6. Run quality checks
456: ```
457: 
458: **After (YAML Pipeline)**:
459: ```yaml
460: document_creation_workflow:
461:   phase_1_analysis:
462:     action: "Analyze request and determine document type"
463:     output: "Document type classification"
464:     validation: "Type must be one of: SKILL, Command, Knowledge, Spec, README"
465: 
466:   phase_2_template_selection:
467:     action: "Select appropriate template based on document type"
468:     output: "Template file path"
469:     depends_on: "phase_1_analysis"
470: 
471:   phase_3_population:
472:     action: "Populate template with user-provided content"
473:     output: "Draft document with filled sections"
474:     depends_on: "phase_2_template_selection"
475: 
476:   phase_4_validation:
477:     action: "Validate structure, frontmatter, section ordering"
478:     output: "Validation report (errors/warnings)"
479:     depends_on: "phase_3_population"
480: 
481:   phase_5_formatting:
482:     action: "Apply code standards (spacing, headers)"
483:     output: "Formatted document"
484:     depends_on: "phase_4_validation"
485: 
486:   phase_6_quality_check:
487:     action: "Review checklist + run AI quality evaluation"
488:     output: "Quality notes and improvement recommendations"
489:     depends_on: "phase_5_formatting"
490: ```
491: 
492: ### YAML Configuration: Feature Flags
493: 
494: **Before (Markdown Table)**:
495: ```markdown
496: | Feature           | Default | Description                         |
497: | ----------------- | ------- | ----------------------------------- |
498: | strict_validation | true    | Enforce all validation rules        |
499: | auto_fix          | false   | Automatically fix formatting issues |
500: | frontmatter_check | true    | Validate frontmatter per document type |
501: ```
502: 
503: **After (YAML Configuration)**:
504: ```yaml
505: feature_flags:
506:   strict_validation:
507:     default: true
508:     description: "Enforce all validation rules without warnings"
509:     values: [true, false]
510: 
511:   auto_fix:
512:     default: false
513:     description: "Automatically fix formatting issues during validation"
514:     values: [true, false]
515:     warning: "Use with caution - may change document semantics"
516: 
517:   frontmatter_check:
518:     default: true
519:     description: "Validate frontmatter fields per document type"
520:     values: [true, false]
521:     enforcement_level: "error"
522: ```
523: 
524: ### YAML Workflow: Multi-Branch Decision Process
525: 
526: **Before (Markdown Prose)**:
527: ```markdown
528: The system should detect when to generate variants:
529: - If user explicitly requests options (shows me options, variations, different approaches)
530: - If complexity is high (7+) and uncertainty signals are present (not sure, what would work)
531: - Otherwise, generate single solution
532: 
533: Variant count depends on complexity:
534: - Simple: 2-3 variants
535: - Standard: 3-5 variants
536: - Complex: 5-10 variants
537: ```
538: 
539: **After (YAML Multi-Branch)**:
540: ```yaml
541: variant_generation_logic:
542:   triggers:
543:     explicit:
544:       keywords: ["show me options", "variations", "different approaches", "multiple designs"]
545:       action: "Generate variants immediately"
546:       priority: "high"
547: 
548:     implicit:
549:       conditions:
550:         - "complexity >= 7"
551:         - "uncertainty_signals present"
552:       uncertainty_signals: ["not sure", "what would work", "best approach"]
553:       action: "Generate variants with uncertainty disclaimer"
554:       priority: "medium"
555: 
556:     default:
557:       action: "Generate single optimal solution"
558:       priority: "low"
559: 
560:   variant_count_guidelines:
561:     simple:
562:       complexity_range: [1, 3]
563:       variant_count: "2-3"
564: 
565:     standard:
566:       complexity_range: [4, 6]
567:       variant_count: "3-5"
568: 
569:     complex:
570:       complexity_range: [7, 10]
571:       variant_count: "5-10"
572: 
573:     user_specified:
574:       action: "Honor user's requested count"
575:       override: true
576: ```

675: ## 9. TEMPLATE GUIDELINES
676: 
677: ### Naming Conventions
678: 
679: **File Names** (kebab-case required):
680: - Format: `[topic]-[type].md`
681: - Use hyphens, not underscores
682: - Lowercase only
683: - Descriptive and specific
684: - Examples:
685:   - ✅ `frontmatter-templates.md`
686:   - ✅ `validation-reference.md`
687:   - ✅ `config-examples.yaml`
688:   - ✅ `packaging-guide.md`
689:   - ❌ `templates.md` (too generic)
690:   - ❌ `FrontmatterTemplates.md` (wrong case)
691:   - ❌ `frontmatter_templates.md` (underscores are not canonical)
692: 
693: **Type-Specific Patterns**:
694: 
695: | Asset Type | Naming Pattern           | Kebab-case Examples          |
696: | ---------- | ------------------------ | ---------------------------- |
697: | Template   | `[content]-templates.md` | `frontmatter-templates.md`   |
698: | Reference  | `[topic]-reference.md`   | `emoji-reference.md`         |
699: | Example    | `[topic]-examples.md`    | `optimization-examples.md`   |
700: | Guide      | `[process]-guide.md`     | `packaging-guide.md`         |
701: | Checklist  | `[topic]-checklist.md`   | `validation-checklist.md`    |
702: 
703: **Section Names**:
704: - Use title case
705: - Be descriptive but concise
706: - Number if sequential: `1. Template Name`
707: 
708: ### Content Organization
709: 
710: **Progressive Disclosure**:
711: 1. **Introduction**: What this is, why it exists (1-2 sentences)
712: 2. **Sections**: Each covers one topic completely
713: 3. **Examples**: Show, don't just tell
714: 4. **Quick Reference**: Summary at end (optional)
715: 
716: **Section Structure**:
717: - **Purpose**: Why this section exists
718: - **Guidelines**: How to use the content
719: - **Template**: Copy-paste starting point
720: - **Example**: Complete working example
721: 
722: ### Formatting Standards
723: 
724: **Code Blocks**:
725: - Always specify language: ` ```yaml `, ` ```markdown `, ` ```bash `
726: - Include comments explaining non-obvious parts
727: - Show complete, runnable examples
728: - Use placeholder values that are obviously placeholders
729: 
730: **Placeholders**:
731: - Format: `[descriptive-name]` or `your-value-here`
732: - Examples:
733:   - ✅ `[skill-name]`, `[feature-description]`, `your-project-name`
734:   - ❌ `xxx`, `placeholder`, `FIXME`
735: 
736: **Lists**:
737: - Use `-` for unordered lists
738: - Use `1.` for ordered lists
739: - Nested lists indent by 2 spaces
740: - Keep items parallel in structure
741: 
742: **Tables**:
743: - Include header row
744: - Align consistently (usually left-aligned)
745: - Keep rows concise (1-2 lines)
746: - Use for comparisons or reference data
747: 
748: ### Writing Style
749: 
750: **Clarity**:
751: - Write for someone unfamiliar with your skill
752: - Define domain-specific terms on first use
753: - Use active voice: "Create the file" not "The file should be created"
754: - Be concise but complete
755: 
756: **Examples**:
757: - Every template should have a complete example
758: - Show real-world usage, not toy examples
759: - Include common variations
760: - Annotate non-obvious parts
761: 
762: **Consistency**:
763: - Use same terminology throughout
764: - Follow patterns from other assets in the skill
765: - Match style of SKILL.md
766: - Use consistent formatting

14: # Skill Asset File Templates - Creation Guidelines
15: 
16: Templates and guidelines for creating asset files in AI agent skills.
17: 
18: ## 1. OVERVIEW
19: 
20: ### Location & Naming
21: 
22: **Location:** `.skilled/skills/[skill-name]/assets/`
23: 
24: **Naming Convention:** kebab-case with the appropriate extension
25: 
26: | ✅ Valid Names | ❌ Invalid Names |
27: |---------------|-----------------|
28: | `frontmatter-templates.md` | `FrontmatterTemplates.md` (PascalCase) |
29: | `config-examples.yaml` | `config_examples.yaml` (snake_case) |
30: | `validation-checklist.md` | `ValidationChecklist.MD` (wrong case) |
31: | `emoji-reference.md` | `emojiReference.md` (camelCase) |
32: 
33: ### When to Create Assets
34: 
35: **Create an asset file when:**
36: - Templates users apply repeatedly
37: - Reference data >50 lines and self-contained
38: - Multiple examples of same pattern exist
39: - Lookup tables or decision matrices needed
40: - Template variations for different scenarios
41: 
42: **Keep in SKILL.md when:**
43: - Content <30 lines
44: - Tightly coupled to workflow logic
45: - Needs to be visible immediately (not progressive disclosure)
46: - Part of core instructions (RULES, WORKFLOW sections)
47: 
48: ---
49: 
50: ## 2. ASSET FILE TYPES
51: 
52: ### Template Files
53: **Purpose**: Provide copy-paste starting points for common tasks
54: 
55: **Naming**: `[content-type]-templates.md`
56: - Example: `frontmatter-templates.md`, `structure-templates.md`
57: 
58: **Structure**:
59: - One template per section
60: - Include field descriptions
61: - Show complete examples
62: - Explain when to use each template
63: 
64: **Use cases**:
65: - Document templates (SKILL.md, commands, knowledge files)
66: - Configuration templates (YAML, JSON)
67: - Code templates (functions, classes, modules)
68: 
69: ### Reference Files
70: **Purpose**: Provide lookup tables, decision trees, or reference data
71: 
72: **Naming**: `[topic]-reference.md`
73: - Example: `emoji-reference.md`, `validation-reference.md`
74: 
75: **Structure**:
76: - Tables or lists for quick lookup
77: - Decision matrices
78: - Classification systems
79: - Standards and conventions
80: 
81: **Use cases**:
82: - Emoji selection guides
83: - File type classifications
84: - Validation rule sets
85: - Naming conventions
86: 
87: ### Example Files
88: **Purpose**: Show working examples of skill outputs
89: 
90: **Naming**: `[topic]-examples.md`
91: - Example: `optimization-examples.md`, `skill-examples.md`
92: 
93: **Structure**:
94: - Before/after comparisons
95: - Annotated examples
96: - Multiple variations
97: - Anti-patterns to avoid
98: 
99: **Use cases**:
100: - Complete skill applications
101: - Common patterns
102: - Edge cases
103: - Quality standards
104: 
105: ### Guide Files
106: **Purpose**: Detailed how-to guides for complex processes
107: 
108: **Naming**: `[process]-guide.md`
109: - Example: `packaging-guide.md`, `distribution-guide.md`
110: 
111: **Structure**:
112: - Step-by-step instructions
113: - Troubleshooting sections
114: - Best practices
115: - Common pitfalls
116: 
117: **Use cases**:
118: - Multi-step processes
119: - Advanced techniques
120: - Workflow deep-dives
121: - Integration guides
122: 
123: ---
124: 
125: ## 3. DOCUMENT STRUCTURE
126: 
127: ### Title and Intro
128: 
129: **CRITICAL: The intro after the H1 title must be 1-2 SHORT sentences only.**
130: 
131: ```markdown
132: ---
133: title: [Title]
134: description: [One-line description - same as intro]
135: trigger_phrases:
136:   - "[distinctive phrase one]"
137:   - "[distinctive phrase two]"
138:   - "[distinctive phrase three]"
139: importance_tier: normal
140: contextType: general
141: version: 1.0.0.0
142: ---
143: 
144: # [Title]
145: 
146: [1-2 SHORT sentences only. Brief hook/summary. NO subsections, NO headers here.]
147: 
148: \## 1. OVERVIEW
149: 
150: ### Purpose
151: 
152: [Why this asset exists]
153: 
154: ### Usage
155: 
156: [How to use this asset - copy instructions, customization notes]
157: 
158: ---
159: 
160: \## 2. [Content Section]
161: 
162: [The actual template/checklist/snippet content]
163: 
164: ---
165: 
166: ## N. Related Resources (optional, if present must be last)
167: 
168: [Links to related files]
169: 
170: ```
171: 
172: Every asset file carries this full 5-field frontmatter block: the Skill Advisor harvests it as routing signal (3-8 lowercase multi-word `trigger_phrases` drawn from the doc's content, `importance_tier` defaults to `normal`, and `contextType` is one of `planning|research|implementation|general`). See [frontmatter-templates.md](../../../sk-create-frontmatter/assets/frontmatter-templates.md) for field rules.
173: 
174: > **WARNING: DO NOT duplicate content between intro and OVERVIEW section.**
175: > The intro is a hook. OVERVIEW provides the details.
176: 
177: #### GOOD Intro Structure
178: 
179: ```markdown
180: # Git Commit Templates
181: 
182: Copy the template that matches the change, fill the fields, and commit.
183: 
184: \## 1. OVERVIEW
185: 
186: ### Purpose
187: 
188: Uniform messages let a reader scan history by intent instead of by author.
189: 
190: ### Usage
191: 
192: Copy the appropriate template based on commit type...
193: 
194: ---
195: 
196: \## 2. COMMIT TEMPLATES
197: ...
198: ```
199: 
200: #### BAD Intro Structure (too long, has subsections)
201: 
202: ```markdown
203: # Git Commit Templates
204: 
205: Copy-paste templates for creating well-structured commit messages.
206: 
207: ### Core Principle    ← WRONG: No headers in intro!
208: Atomic commits with clear intent = maintainable history.
209: 
210: ### When to Use       ← WRONG: This belongs in OVERVIEW section!
211: - Creating new features
212: - Fixing bugs
213: 
214: ---
215: ```
216: 
217: ### Intro vs OVERVIEW Content Placement
218: 
219: | Content Type          | Intro (after H1) | OVERVIEW Section       |
220: | --------------------- | ---------------- | ---------------------- |
221: | 1-2 sentence summary  | ✅ YES            | ❌ NO (don't repeat)    |
222: | Core Principle        | ❌ NO             | ✅ YES (in Purpose)     |
223: | When to Use           | ❌ NO             | ✅ YES (in Purpose)     |
224: | How to copy/customize | ❌ NO             | ✅ YES (in Usage)       |
225: | Prerequisites         | ❌ NO             | ✅ YES (in Usage)       |
226: | Any H2/H3 subsections | ❌ NEVER          | ✅ YES                  |
227: 
228: ---
229: 
230: ## 4. STANDARD ASSET STRUCTURE
231: 
232: **Template**:
233: 
234: ````markdown
235: ---
236: title: Asset Title - Descriptive Subtitle
237: description: One-line description of what this asset provides
238: trigger_phrases:
239:   - "[distinctive phrase one]"
240:   - "[distinctive phrase two]"
241:   - "[distinctive phrase three]"
242: importance_tier: normal
243: contextType: general
244: version: 1.0.0.0
245: ---
246: 
247: # Asset Title - Descriptive Subtitle
248: 
249: Brief introduction (1-2 sentences) explaining what this asset provides and when to use it.
250: 
251: \## 1. OVERVIEW
252: 
253: ### Purpose
254: 
255: [Why this asset exists, what problem it solves]
256: 
257: ### Usage
258: 
259: [How to use this asset - copy instructions, customization notes]
260: 
261: ---
262: 
263: \## 2. SECTION NAME
264: 
265: **Key Points**:
266: - Point 1
267: - Point 2
268: - Point 3
269: 
270: **Template**:
271: ```[language]
272: # Template content here
273: # With explanatory comments
274: ```
275: 
276: **Field Guidelines**:
277: 
278: **`field_name`**:
279: - Description of field
280: - Format requirements
281: - Example: `value-example`
282: 
283: **Complete Example**:
284: ```[language]
285: # Complete working example
286: # Ready to copy and adapt
287: ```
288: 
289: ---
290: 
291: \## 3. SECTION NAME
292: 
293: [Continue pattern...]
294: 
295: ---
296: 
297: ## N. RELATED RESOURCES
298: 
299: [Links to related files - MUST be last section if present]
300: 
301: ````
302: 
303: ---
304: 
305: ## 5. LOGIC REPRESENTATION PATTERNS
306: 
307: **Purpose**: Guidelines for representing logic, workflows, and decision trees in asset files using structured formats instead of prose.
308: 
309: **Why Structured Logic?**
310: - **Clarity**: Executable-style logic is easier to understand than prose
311: - **AI-Friendly**: LLMs parse structured logic better than narrative descriptions
312: - **Maintainability**: Changes to logic are more visible in structured formats
313: - **Consistency**: Same patterns across all asset files
314: 
315: ### When to Use Each Format
316: 
317: **Use Python Pseudo-Code When:**
318: - Complex branching logic (multiple IF/ELIF/ELSE conditions)
319: - Function/method definitions with clear inputs/outputs
320: - State management or algorithmic processes
321: - Validation or transformation logic
322: - Examples: Mode detection, validation pipelines, decision functions
323: 
324: **Use YAML Structures When:**
325: - Configuration data (settings, options, parameters)
326: - Pipeline definitions (multi-step workflows with clear phases)
327: - Hierarchical workflows (nested processes)
328: - Metadata structures (categorization, tagging)
329: - Examples: Workflow definitions, configuration templates, feature matrices
330: 
331: **Use Markdown Decision Trees When:**
332: - Simple branching logic (2-5 branches)
333: - Visual flow representation (user-facing paths)
334: - Classification systems (type determination)
335: - Quick decision guides
336: - Examples: Document type selection, frontmatter requirements
337: 
338: **Keep Markdown Prose When:**
339: - Explanatory text and conceptual overviews
340: - Narrative examples with context
341: - Best practices guidance
342: - Introductions and summaries
343: 
344: ---
345: 
346: ## 6. DECISION LOGIC EXAMPLES
347: 
348: **Purpose**: Demonstrate how to convert markdown prose into structured decision logic.
349: 
350: ### Python Pseudo-Code: Mode Detection
351: 
352: **Before (Markdown Prose)**:
353: ```markdown
354: Check user input for mode indicators:
355: - If "$quick" is present, use quick mode with auto-scaling depth
356: - If "$ticket" is present, use ticket mode with depth 10
357: - Otherwise, use interactive mode with depth 10
358: ```
359: 
360: **After (Python Pseudo-Code)**:
361: ```python
362: def detect_mode(request):
363:     """Detect execution mode from user request markers"""
364: 
365:     if '$quick' in request:
366:         mode = 'quick'
367:         depth = 'auto_scale_1_to_5'
368:     elif '$ticket' in request:
369:         mode = 'ticket'
370:         depth = 'depth_10_rounds'
371:     else:
372:         # DEFAULT TO INTERACTIVE
373:         mode = 'interactive'
374:         depth = 'depth_10_rounds'
375: 
376:     return mode, depth
377: ```
378: 
379: ### Markdown Decision Tree: Frontmatter Requirements
380: 
381: **Before (Markdown Prose)**:
382: ```markdown
383: Different document types have different frontmatter requirements:
384: - SKILL.md files must have frontmatter with name, description, allowed-tools, and version
385: - Command files must have frontmatter with description and argument-hint
386: - Skill reference/asset files must have the 5-field block
387: - Knowledge files outside skill folders should not have frontmatter
388: - Spec files typically don't have frontmatter
389: ```
390: 
391: **After (Markdown Decision Tree)**:
392: ```
393: Document type?
394: ├─> SKILL.md             → MUST have frontmatter (name, description, allowed-tools, version)
395: ├─> Command              → MUST have frontmatter (description, argument-hint, allowed-tools)
396: ├─> Skill Reference/Asset → MUST have the 5-field block (title, description,
397: │                           trigger_phrases, importance_tier, contextType)
398: ├─> Knowledge (outside skills) → MUST NOT have frontmatter (remove if present)
399: ├─> Spec                 → SHOULD NOT have frontmatter (suggest removal)
400: └─> README               → No specific requirement (usually none)
401: ```
402: 
403: ### Python Pseudo-Code: Validation Logic
404: 
405: **Before (Markdown Prose)**:
406: ```markdown
407: Validate the document structure:
408: 1. Check if required sections exist
409: 2. Verify section ordering is correct
410: 3. Ensure frontmatter is valid (if present)
411: ```
412: 
413: **After (Python Pseudo-Code)**:
414: ```python
415: def validate_document(doc, doc_type):
416:     """Validate document structure and content"""
417: 
418:     errors = []
419: 
420:     # Check required sections
421:     required_sections = get_required_sections(doc_type)
422:     for section in required_sections:
423:         if section not in doc.sections:
424:             errors.append(f"Missing required section: {section}")
425: 
426:     # Verify section ordering
427:     expected_order = get_section_order(doc_type)
428:     actual_order = [s.name for s in doc.sections]
429:     if actual_order != expected_order:
430:         errors.append(f"Section order incorrect. Expected: {expected_order}")
431: 
432:     # Validate frontmatter
433:     if doc.has_frontmatter:
434:         frontmatter_errors = validate_frontmatter(doc.frontmatter, doc_type)
435:         errors.extend(frontmatter_errors)
436: 
437:     return errors
438: ```
439: 
440: ---
441: 
442: ## 7. WORKFLOW PATTERNS
443: 
444: **Purpose**: Show how to represent multi-step workflows using YAML structures.
445: 
446: ### YAML Pipeline: Document Creation Workflow
447: 
448: **Before (Markdown List)**:
449: ```markdown
450: 1. Analyze the request and determine document type
451: 2. Select appropriate template
452: 3. Populate template with content
453: 4. Validate structure and content
454: 5. Apply formatting standards
455: 6. Run quality checks
456: ```
457: 
458: **After (YAML Pipeline)**:
459: ```yaml
460: document_creation_workflow:
461:   phase_1_analysis:
462:     action: "Analyze request and determine document type"
463:     output: "Document type classification"
464:     validation: "Type must be one of: SKILL, Command, Knowledge, Spec, README"
465: 
466:   phase_2_template_selection:
467:     action: "Select appropriate template based on document type"
468:     output: "Template file path"
469:     depends_on: "phase_1_analysis"
470: 
471:   phase_3_population:
472:     action: "Populate template with user-provided content"
473:     output: "Draft document with filled sections"
474:     depends_on: "phase_2_template_selection"
475: 
476:   phase_4_validation:
477:     action: "Validate structure, frontmatter, section ordering"
478:     output: "Validation report (errors/warnings)"
479:     depends_on: "phase_3_population"
480: 
481:   phase_5_formatting:
482:     action: "Apply code standards (spacing, headers)"
483:     output: "Formatted document"
484:     depends_on: "phase_4_validation"
485: 
486:   phase_6_quality_check:
487:     action: "Review checklist + run AI quality evaluation"
488:     output: "Quality notes and improvement recommendations"
489:     depends_on: "phase_5_formatting"
490: ```
491: 
492: ### YAML Configuration: Feature Flags
493: 
494: **Before (Markdown Table)**:
495: ```markdown
496: | Feature           | Default | Description                         |
497: | ----------------- | ------- | ----------------------------------- |
498: | strict_validation | true    | Enforce all validation rules        |
499: | auto_fix          | false   | Automatically fix formatting issues |
500: | frontmatter_check | true    | Validate frontmatter per document type |
501: ```
502: 
503: **After (YAML Configuration)**:
504: ```yaml
505: feature_flags:
506:   strict_validation:
507:     default: true
508:     description: "Enforce all validation rules without warnings"
509:     values: [true, false]
510: 
511:   auto_fix:
512:     default: false
513:     description: "Automatically fix formatting issues during validation"
514:     values: [true, false]
515:     warning: "Use with caution - may change document semantics"
516: 
517:   frontmatter_check:
518:     default: true
519:     description: "Validate frontmatter fields per document type"
520:     values: [true, false]
521:     enforcement_level: "error"
522: ```
523: 
524: ### YAML Workflow: Multi-Branch Decision Process
525: 
526: **Before (Markdown Prose)**:
527: ```markdown
528: The system should detect when to generate variants:
529: - If user explicitly requests options (shows me options, variations, different approaches)
530: - If complexity is high (7+) and uncertainty signals are present (not sure, what would work)
531: - Otherwise, generate single solution
532: 
533: Variant count depends on complexity:
534: - Simple: 2-3 variants
535: - Standard: 3-5 variants
536: - Complex: 5-10 variants
537: ```
538: 
539: **After (YAML Multi-Branch)**:
540: ```yaml
541: variant_generation_logic:
542:   triggers:
543:     explicit:
544:       keywords: ["show me options", "variations", "different approaches", "multiple designs"]
545:       action: "Generate variants immediately"
546:       priority: "high"
547: 
548:     implicit:
549:       conditions:
550:         - "complexity >= 7"
551:         - "uncertainty_signals present"
552:       uncertainty_signals: ["not sure", "what would work", "best approach"]
553:       action: "Generate variants with uncertainty disclaimer"
554:       priority: "medium"
555: 
556:     default:
557:       action: "Generate single optimal solution"
558:       priority: "low"
559: 
560:   variant_count_guidelines:
561:     simple:
562:       complexity_range: [1, 3]
563:       variant_count: "2-3"
564: 
565:     standard:
566:       complexity_range: [4, 6]
567:       variant_count: "3-5"
568: 
569:     complex:
570:       complexity_range: [7, 10]
571:       variant_count: "5-10"
572: 
573:     user_specified:
574:       action: "Honor user's requested count"
575:       override: true
576: ```

578: ---
579: 
580: ## 8. CONFIGURATION TEMPLATES
581: 
582: **Purpose**: Demonstrate structured data formats for configuration and metadata.
583: 
584: ### YAML: Tool Configuration
585: 
586: ```yaml

675: ## 9. TEMPLATE GUIDELINES
676: 
677: ### Naming Conventions
678: 
679: **File Names** (kebab-case required):
680: - Format: `[topic]-[type].md`
681: - Use hyphens, not underscores
682: - Lowercase only
683: - Descriptive and specific
684: - Examples:
685:   - ✅ `frontmatter-templates.md`
686:   - ✅ `validation-reference.md`
687:   - ✅ `config-examples.yaml`
688:   - ✅ `packaging-guide.md`
689:   - ❌ `templates.md` (too generic)
690:   - ❌ `FrontmatterTemplates.md` (wrong case)
691:   - ❌ `frontmatter_templates.md` (underscores are not canonical)
692: 
693: **Type-Specific Patterns**:
694: 
695: | Asset Type | Naming Pattern           | Kebab-case Examples          |
696: | ---------- | ------------------------ | ---------------------------- |
697: | Template   | `[content]-templates.md` | `frontmatter-templates.md`   |
698: | Reference  | `[topic]-reference.md`   | `emoji-reference.md`         |
699: | Example    | `[topic]-examples.md`    | `optimization-examples.md`   |
700: | Guide      | `[process]-guide.md`     | `packaging-guide.md`         |
701: | Checklist  | `[topic]-checklist.md`   | `validation-checklist.md`    |
702: 
703: **Section Names**:
704: - Use title case
705: - Be descriptive but concise
706: - Number if sequential: `1. Template Name`
707: 
708: ### Content Organization
709: 
710: **Progressive Disclosure**:

12: # sk-design-fundamentals
13: 
14: > A UI that reads as designed, because every value came from a list instead of a guess.
15: 
16: Most interfaces built by people who do not consider themselves designers fail the same way. Nothing is individually wrong. The padding is 17px because it looked about right, the blue came from a color picker, the shadow was copied from a component library, and the transition is 400ms because 400 is a round number. Each choice is defensible alone. Together they read as amateur, and nobody can say why.

18: ---
19: 
20: ## 1. AT A GLANCE
21: 
22: | Aspect | What you get |
23: |---|---|
24: | **Use it for** | Deciding UI values and behavior when building, fixing or reviewing an interface. |
25: | **Invoke with** | "make this look better", "looks off", "spacing scale", "color palette", "focus ring", "animation duration", "design review". |
26: | **Works on** | Any web or app surface: a component, a screen, a described complaint, or a set of files. |
27: | **Produces** | Concrete values and CSS with the reason each was chosen, or severity-tiered review findings with file, line and fix. |
28: 
29: ---
30: 
31: ## 2. OVERVIEW
32: 
33: ### Why This Skill Exists
34: 
35: Visual design gets treated as talent, so people who do not have it guess. Guessing produces 35 slightly different blues, spacing that never quite groups anything, and a headline that is enormous on a phone. The fix is not taste. It is a small set of decisions made once, which sixteen spacing values exist, which eleven font sizes, which nine shades of each color, after which every later choice is picking from a list. That is what this skill carries, along with the techniques for building hierarchy, the interaction details that make a screen behave under a real thumb, and the motion model that keeps it from feeling either sluggish or cartoonish.
36: 
37: ### What It Does
38: 
39: The skill decides values and behavior for a surface. `SKILL.md` holds the scales themselves, the procedure for working, and the four hierarchy rules that do most of the visible work. `references/hierarchy.md` carries the full method. Seven references carry the rest: hierarchy technique, palette construction, a symptom-to-fix table for existing UI, depth and typography technique, interaction craft, motion principles, and a WCAG-cited review checklist.
40: 
41: It is the authoring counterpart to `sk-design-md-generator`, which measures a live site's real CSS into a Style Reference. That skill reads a surface; this one writes one. When a measured reference exists, its values win.
42: 
43: ### Why It Matters
44: 
45: - **Fewer decisions, better results:** picking from sixteen spacing values is faster than typing a number, and the result is consistent by construction.
46: - **Vague complaints become fixable:** "looks off" maps to a named cause with a named fix, instead of a restyling session.
47: - **Accessibility is not an afterthought:** contrast minimums, focus rings, touch targets and keyboard behavior are in the same rules as the visual ones.
48: 
49: ### The Design Knowledge Layer
50: 
51: The skill distills four public sources into one operating model, kept in the order a task actually moves: choose values, build hierarchy, implement behavior, animate, verify.
52: 
53: | Layer | What the skill knows how to operate |
54: |---|---|
55: | Value scales | Spacing, type, weight, color, elevation, radius, opacity and duration, as fixed lists with the reasoning for each. |
56: | Procedure | The order of work for something new: feature before layout, grayscale before color, mobile before desktop. |
57: | Hierarchy | Primary, secondary and tertiary tiers built through weight and color, and the emphasize-by-de-emphasizing technique. |
58: | Color construction | Nine-shade HSL ramps, saturation at the ends, hue rotation, dark mode, and two escape hatches for contrast. |
59: | Interaction craft | Inputs, touch, hit areas, focus rings, keyboard, screen readers, performance and feedback placement. |
60: | Motion | The twelve animation principles adapted to UI, with enforceable timing, easing, physics and staging values. |
61: | UX laws | Target sizing, choice count, chunking, the 400ms response budget, grouping and emphasis. |
62: | Review | A severity-tiered pass over UI code with WCAG criteria, producing file, line and fix. |
63: 
64: ---
65: 
66: ## 3. QUICK START
67: 
68: **Step 1: Invoke it.** Routing is automatic on the trigger phrases above. To load it manually:
69: 
70: ```bash
71: cat .skilled/skills/sk-design/sk-design-fundamentals/SKILL.md
72: ```
73: 
74: The scales in Section 3 are the always-loaded part; everything else loads on intent.
75: 
76: **Step 2: Take the token file.**
77: 
78: ```bash
79: cp .skilled/skills/sk-design/sk-design-fundamentals/assets/tokens.css <your-project>/styles/tokens.css
80: ```
81: 
82: You get every scale as CSS custom properties, a semantic role layer, and a dark-mode block. Retune the hues rather than rebuilding the ramps.
83: 
84: **Step 3: Verify the skill package before relying on it.**
85: 
86: ```bash
87: python3 .skilled/skills/sk-doc/sk-create-skill/scripts/validate_skill_package.py .skilled/skills/sk-design
88: ```
89: 
90: Exit 0 with no hard failures.
91: 
92: ---
93: 
94: ## 4. HOW IT WORKS
95: 
96: A request arrives and the router asks one question first: is there nothing yet, a complaint, or existing code? That answer decides which reference loads before anything else happens. From there the work follows the same four phases regardless of entry point: choose values from the scales, establish hierarchy, implement behavior, then verify against the hard rules and contrast minimums.
97: 
98: ```text
99: [UI request]
100:    |
101:    v
102: [build? improve? review?]
103:    |                 |                    |
104:    v                 v                    v
105: [scales in       [diagnosis-table    [review-checklist
106:  SKILL.md]        maps symptom]       scans the code]
107:    |                 |                    |
108:    +--------+--------+--------------------+
109:             v
110:    [hierarchy, interaction, motion]  -->  [values + reasons, or findings]
111: ```
112: 
113: ### Values Outrank Adjectives
114: 
115: The output is never "make the spacing tighter". It is `--space-4` instead of `--space-5`, with the reason: more space around a group than within it. That is what makes the result implementable by `sk-code` without another round of interpretation.
116: 
117: ### Sources Disagree, And The Skill Says So
118: 
119: Four sources went into this skill and they do not agree everywhere. Fluid `clamp()` sizing conflicts with a fixed type scale. Three different motion-duration ceilings exist. Touch-target minimums differ by 12px. One source calls pure-black shadows harsh while another's default elevation scale uses them. Each conflict is stated where it lands, with a resolution and the reasoning, rather than quietly picking a winner.
120: 
121: The same applies across skills: `sk-design-md-generator` records type ratios and motion bands as targets for *reading* a measured surface, which would look like a contradiction if direction were ignored. Both skills now carry the reconciliation, so neither can be read in isolation and misapplied.
122: 
123: ---
124: 
125: ## 5. INTEGRATION & NAVIGATION
126: 
127: ### When To Use This Skill
128: 
129: - Building a component or screen and needing to decide sizes, colors, shadows or durations.
130: - Someone says the UI looks off, cluttered, plain or unfinished.
131: - Reviewing a pull request that touches UI, and the review must produce findings rather than impressions.
132: - Extending an existing palette to a new accent or to dark mode.
133: 
134: Do not use it to document a live site's existing CSS. That is extraction and belongs to `sk-design-md-generator`.
135: 
136: ### Related Skills
137: 
138: | Skill | Relationship |
139: |---|---|
140: | `sk-design-md-generator` | Measures an existing surface into a Style Reference. Its measured values outrank this skill's defaults; both skills state the boundary. |
141: | `sk-code` | Implements the values this skill decides. |
142: | `system-spec-kit` | Owns packet documentation and continuity when the work is tracked. |
143: 
144: ---
145: 
146: ## 6. TROUBLESHOOTING
147: 
148: | What you see | Why | Fix |
149: |---|---|---|
150: | Suggested values conflict with the project's tokens | The project has an established system this skill does not know about | Point the skill at the token file. An established system outranks these defaults. |
151: | A color cannot reach 4.5:1 | The brand color is too light for its role | Use one of the two escape hatches in `references/color-system.md`, or escalate the brand color as an operator decision. |
152: | A fix makes another element fail contrast | De-emphasizing a competitor pushed its text below the minimum | Re-run the contrast check after every hierarchy change; the hard rules apply after the fix, not only before it. |
153: | Motion guidance seems contradictory | Sources use different ceilings for different kinds of motion | See `references/motion-principles.md` Section 5, which separates feedback, state change and layout transition. |
154: 
155: ---
156: 
157: ## 7. FAQ
158: 
159: **Q: Why not just use a component library?**
160: 
161: A: A library gives you components, not the decisions behind them. It cannot tell you which of its shadows belongs on this element, or why the page still reads as noise once the components are in place.
162: 
163: **Q: The skill is named after design, but half of it is accessibility and motion. Why?**
164: 
165: A: Because a surface that looks right and behaves wrong is not finished. Contrast, focus, touch targets and durations are values like any other, so they live on the same scales and in the same rules.
166: 
167: **Q: How does this differ from `sk-design-md-generator`?**
168: 
169: A: That skill measures what a live site already does. This one decides what a surface should do when nothing has been decided yet. They are the reading and writing halves of the same job.

91: 
92: ---
93: 
94: ## 4. HOW IT WORKS
95: 
96: A request arrives and the router asks one question first: is there nothing yet, a complaint, or existing code? That answer decides which reference loads before anything else happens. From there the work follows the same four phases regardless of entry point: choose values from the scales, establish hierarchy, implement behavior, then verify against the hard rules and contrast minimums.
97: 
98: ```text
99: [UI request]
100:    |
101:    v
102: [build? improve? review?]
103:    |                 |                    |
104:    v                 v                    v
105: [scales in       [diagnosis-table    [review-checklist
106:  SKILL.md]        maps symptom]       scans the code]
107:    |                 |                    |
108:    +--------+--------+--------------------+
109:             v
110:    [hierarchy, interaction, motion]  -->  [values + reasons, or findings]
111: ```
112: 
113: ### Values Outrank Adjectives
114: 
115: The output is never "make the spacing tighter". It is `--space-4` instead of `--space-5`, with the reason: more space around a group than within it. That is what makes the result implementable by `sk-code` without another round of interpretation.
116: 
117: ### Sources Disagree, And The Skill Says So
118: 
119: Four sources went into this skill and they do not agree everywhere. Fluid `clamp()` sizing conflicts with a fixed type scale. Three different motion-duration ceilings exist. Touch-target minimums differ by 12px. One source calls pure-black shadows harsh while another's default elevation scale uses them. Each conflict is stated where it lands, with a resolution and the reasoning, rather than quietly picking a winner.
120: 
121: The same applies across skills: `sk-design-md-generator` records type ratios and motion bands as targets for *reading* a measured surface, which would look like a contradiction if direction were ignored. Both skills now carry the reconciliation, so neither can be read in isolation and misapplied.
122: 
123: ---
124: 
125: ## 5. INTEGRATION & NAVIGATION
126: 
127: ### When To Use This Skill
128: 
129: - Building a component or screen and needing to decide sizes, colors, shadows or durations.
130: - Someone says the UI looks off, cluttered, plain or unfinished.
131: - Reviewing a pull request that touches UI, and the review must produce findings rather than impressions.
132: - Extending an existing palette to a new accent or to dark mode.
133: 
134: Do not use it to document a live site's existing CSS. That is extraction and belongs to `sk-design-md-generator`.
135: 
136: ### Related Skills
137: 
138: | Skill | Relationship |
139: |---|---|
140: | `sk-design-md-generator` | Measures an existing surface into a Style Reference. Its measured values outrank this skill's defaults; both skills state the boundary. |
141: | `sk-code` | Implements the values this skill decides. |
142: | `system-spec-kit` | Owns packet documentation and continuity when the work is tracked. |
143: 
144: ---
145: 
146: ## 6. TROUBLESHOOTING
147: 
148: | What you see | Why | Fix |
149: |---|---|---|
150: | Suggested values conflict with the project's tokens | The project has an established system this skill does not know about | Point the skill at the token file. An established system outranks these defaults. |
151: | A color cannot reach 4.5:1 | The brand color is too light for its role | Use one of the two escape hatches in `references/color-system.md`, or escalate the brand color as an operator decision. |
152: | A fix makes another element fail contrast | De-emphasizing a competitor pushed its text below the minimum | Re-run the contrast check after every hierarchy change; the hard rules apply after the fix, not only before it. |
153: | Motion guidance seems contradictory | Sources use different ceilings for different kinds of motion | See `references/motion-principles.md` Section 5, which separates feedback, state change and layout transition. |
154: 
155: ---
156: 
157: ## 7. FAQ
158: 
159: **Q: Why not just use a component library?**
160: 
161: A: A library gives you components, not the decisions behind them. It cannot tell you which of its shadows belongs on this element, or why the page still reads as noise once the components are in place.
162: 
163: **Q: The skill is named after design, but half of it is accessibility and motion. Why?**
164: 
165: A: Because a surface that looks right and behaves wrong is not finished. Contrast, focus, touch targets and durations are values like any other, so they live on the same scales and in the same rules.
166: 
167: **Q: How does this differ from `sk-design-md-generator`?**
168: 
169: A: That skill measures what a live site already does. This one decides what a surface should do when nothing has been decided yet. They are the reading and writing halves of the same job.

8: # Visual Design
9: 
10: Visual design is not talent. It is a small set of systems decisions made **once**, plus a handful of
11: techniques for building hierarchy, a set of interaction details that make a screen behave correctly,
12: and a motion model that keeps it feeling human.
13: 
14: **Most of that is not about screens.** A spacing scale, a type scale, a colour ramp and a hierarchy
15: pyramid decide a slide, a printed page and a report layout as much as they decide a component. The
16: sections below say which parts carry to every surface and which are genuinely screen-only, so a deck
17: question gets the systems and skips the focus rings.
18: 
19: The single biggest cause of amateur-looking UI is picking values ad hoc — 17px here, `#3B82F6` there, `lighten(5%)` for a hover state, `400ms` because it seemed smooth. Design *from a scale*, always.
20: 
21: > **Boundary.** This skill decides values and behavior when UI is being **built, fixed, or reviewed**. It is prescriptive and emits CSS. 70: ## 3. HOW IT WORKS
71: 
72: ### The Surfaces
73: 
74: The systems below are surface-agnostic. What differs is which of the extras apply.
75: 
76: | Surface | Systems that apply | What changes | What does not apply |
77: | --- | --- | --- | --- |
78: | **Screen UI** | All four | The reference surface these rules were written against | Nothing |
79: | **Slide decks** | All four | Far fewer elements per view, so hierarchy does more work and the type scale runs larger. Transitions replace interaction motion | Focus rings, hover, touch targets |
80: | **Printed layouts** | All four | No dark mode and no hover state. Contrast still matters and is harder, because paper has no backlight. Measure in a physical unit and keep the spacing ratios | Interaction craft, motion, response budgets |
81: | **Document layouts** | All four | Reading order is the hierarchy. Long-form type scale runs tighter than UI, and white space carries the structure | Interaction craft, motion |
82: | **Chart and diagram canvases** | Colour and type scale only | Those canvases have their own layout rules | Everything else; the canvas modes own it |
83: 
84: Two references are screen-only: [`interaction-craft.md`](references/interaction-craft.md) and
85: [`motion-principles.md`](references/motion-principles.md). A deck may borrow the motion timings for
86: transitions; a printed page has no use for either. Everything else in `references/` applies whatever
87: the surface.
88: 
89: ### The Systems
90: 
91: Pick from these lists. Never invent a value that is not on one.
92: 
93: #### Spacing and sizing
94: 
95: Base 16px, built from factors and multiples of it:
96: 
97: ```text
98: 4  8  12  16  24  32  48  64  96  128  192  256  384  512  640  768
99: ```
100: 
101: Tight at the small end, spreading out at the large end. **No two adjacent values may be closer than about 25%** — that is what makes the choice obvious. A linear "multiples of 4" scale fails, because it does not help anyone decide between 120px and 124px.
102: 
103: Use it for margin, padding, width, height, icon sizes and border width — everything spatial. Fix a small set of opacity values too (`.05 .1 .2 .4 .6 .8`) for disabled states, overlays and hover tints, rather than eyeballing a slider each time. Same logic as the other scales: decide once, reuse everywhere.
104: 
105: #### Type scale
106: 
107: ```text
108: 12  14  16  18  20  24  30  36  48  60  72
109: ```
110: 
111: Not a modular scale built from a ratio. Ratios produce fractional pixel values that round inconsistently across browsers, and they are too sparse for interface density. Hand-picked values, chosen for how they feel, win instead.
112: 
113: **Units: `px` or `rem` only. Never `em`.** `em` is relative to the current font size, so `.875em` inside a `1.25em` parent computes to 17.5px — a value not on the scale. The scale silently stops existing.
114: 
115: #### Font weight
116: 
117: Two weights is enough:
118: 
119: - **400 or 500** for body and most UI text.
120: - **600 or 700** for anything emphasized. Medium-sized headings usually sit best at 500 to 600.
121: 
122: Nothing below 400 in UI. To de-emphasize, use a lighter *color* or a smaller *size*, never a lighter weight. Weight must also not change on hover or selection, because the width change shifts the layout.
123: 
124: #### Color
125: 
126: A five-swatch palette generator gives nowhere near enough colors.
127: 
128: - **Greys: 8 to 10 shades.** Almost all of a UI is grey — text, backgrounds, panels, borders, form controls. Three or four shades always runs out. Start at a very dark grey, not true black, which looks unnatural.
129: - **Primary: 5 to 10 shades**, one or at most two primaries.
130: - **Accents: 5 to 10 shades each** — destructive red, warning yellow, positive green, plus whatever else the product must distinguish. Ten colors at 5 to 10 shades each is normal for a complex UI.
131: 
132: Name them `100` (lightest) through `900` (darkest), base `500`.
133: 
134: **Build the ramp in one order:** base `500` first, then the `900` and `100` edges, then the gap fills — the reasoning, and the button-background test that decides `500`, are in [`references/color-system.md`](references/color-system.md) Section 3.
135: 
136: **Write colors as HSL, not hex.** `hsl(220, 95%, 34%)` and `hsl(220, 65%, 61%)` are visibly related; `#03369E` and `#507DD7` are not.
137: 
138: **Never generate shades at runtime** with `lighten()` or `darken()`. That is how a project ends up with 35 slightly different blues.
139: 
140: Full construction method — base selection, saturation at the ends, hue rotation, dark mode, contrast escape hatches — is in [`references/color-system.md`](references/color-system.md).
141: 
142: #### Shadows, five elevations
143: 
144: ```css
145: 0 1px 3px   hsla(0,0%,0%,.2)   /* barely raised - buttons */
146: 0 4px 6px   hsla(0,0%,0%,.2)   /* dropdowns */
147: 0 5px 15px  hsla(0,0%,0%,.2)
148: 0 10px 24px hsla(0,0%,0%,.2)
149: 0 15px 35px hsla(0,0%,0%,.2)   /* modals */
150: ```
151: 
152: Choose by asking *where on the z-axis does this sit?*, not *what shadow looks nice?*. Closer to the user means more attention. Shrinking a button's shadow on `:active` makes it feel pressed. Growing a list item's shadow when it is picked up for drag-to-reorder does the reverse — it reads as "now above its siblings" and doubles as the drag affordance.
153: 
154: Every shadow in a project shares one offset direction, because there is one light source. [`references/depth-and-detail.md`](references/depth-and-detail.md) carries two refined alternatives:
155: 
156: - a **two-part** cast-plus-contact scale
157: - a **layered** three-part set
158: 
159: It also carries the rule for tinting shadow color on non-white surfaces, and the full six-layer button anatomy. The three systems are parallel and not compatible. Pick one per project and never mix them, or elevation stops being readable.
160: 
161: #### Line-height and line length
162: 
163: Line-height is **inversely** proportional to font size, and proportional to line width:
164: 
165: - small text or wide columns: `1.5` to `2`
166: - large headlines: `1` is fine
167: 
168: Line length: **45 to 75 characters**, which is `max-width: 20em` to `35em`. This applies to the paragraph even when its container is wider. Mixed widths in one content area look more polished, not less.
169: 
170: `em` is correct *here* — measure should scale with the text it wraps. The "never `em`" rule is scoped to the *type scale*, where `em` compounds through nesting. Do not "fix" this.
171: 
172: #### Border radius
173: 
174: Pick one and stay consistent. Small radius reads neutral, large reads playful, none reads serious or formal. Mixing square and rounded corners in one interface always looks worse. For nested elements, inner radius equals outer radius minus the padding between them.
175: 
176: #### Motion durations
177: 
178: Timing is a scale like the others, and consistency across it outranks the perfect value for any one element.
179: 
180: ```text
181: 120-180ms   press, hover, direct feedback
182: 180-260ms   small state change: toggle, dropdown, tooltip, tab
183: up to 500ms layout transition: modal, drawer, accordion
184: ```
185: 
186: 300ms is the ceiling for anything the user initiated. Similar elements use identical values. The full model — easing curves, springs, staging, and when not to animate at all — is in [`references/motion-principles.md`](references/motion-principles.md).
187: 
188: ### The Procedure
189: 
190: Seven steps govern the order of work on something new: start from a feature rather than a layout, work in **grayscale first**, treat low-fidelity artifacts as disposable, build the smallest useful version, **choose each value by elimination** against its two neighbours on the scale, start with too much white space and trim, and design at about 400px before relaxing to a large screen.
191: 
192: Full steps with their reasoning: [`references/build-procedure.md`](references/build-procedure.md). Load it when starting something new; a value question does not need it.
193: 
194: ### Hierarchy, The Technique That Does The Most Work
195: 
196: Everything on the surface sits in a pyramid: primary, secondary, tertiary. When everything competes, the surface reads as noise. This is the most surface-agnostic technique here: a slide with three competing headings fails the same way a screen does. This is what makes a design look designed, not styling.
197: 
198: Four rules carry most of it:
199: 
200: - **size is not everything**: weight and color carry the emphasis, with sizes kept near the middle of the scale
201: - **three text colors, maximum**: all three at 4.5:1
202: - **emphasize by de-emphasizing**: soften the competition rather than amplifying the primary
203: - **style actions by hierarchy, not by semantics**
204: 
205: The full method is in [`references/hierarchy.md`](references/hierarchy.md) Sections 2 through 7. It covers the destructive-action treatment, label suppression, the weight-versus-contrast trade, and why visual hierarchy may disagree with document hierarchy.
206: 
207: ### Beyond The Visual System
208: 
209: Correct values do not make a screen behave correctly. Six references carry the behavior, each on its own intent:

212: - [`hierarchy.md`](references/hierarchy.md) Sections 1 and 3
213: - [`interaction-craft.md`](references/interaction-craft.md) Sections 3 and 5
214: - [`motion-principles.md`](references/motion-principles.md) Section 4
215: - [`ux-laws.md`](references/ux-laws.md) Sections 2 to 5
216: - [`review-checklist.md`](references/review-checklist.md) Sections 2 to 6

An unknown or unnamed project loads none, and the slot adds no routing phrase, since naming the project is what reaches it. When sources disagree, the order is:

222: 1. The repository's mode.
223: 2. The tokens the app installs.
224: 3. The design scales in this file.
225: 4. The profile.
226: 
227: ---
228: 
229: ## 4. RULES
230: 
231: ### ✅ ALWAYS
232: 
233: 1. **ALWAYS pick values from the scales in Section 3.** A value off the scale is the defect this skill exists to prevent; it is what makes a UI read as amateur even when nothing is individually wrong. Timing is a scale too.
234: 2. **ALWAYS put more space around a group than within it.** This is the fix for "which label belongs to which field", cramped bullet lists (the gap must exceed the line-height), and headings that look attached to the wrong paragraph. Ambiguous spacing is a functional bug, not only an ugly one.
235: 3. **ALWAYS meet 4.5:1 for normal text.** The 3:1 allowance applies only to *large* text, which WCAG defines as **24px regular or 18.66px bold**, not 18px.
236:     - **3:1 applies to non-text** (WCAG 1.4.11). A border that is the only thing identifying a control, such as an input outline or a checkbox edge, needs 3:1 against its background.
237:     - A hairline that merely divides content does not. Text and non-text are two different tokens.
238: 4. **ALWAYS give large elements a faster shrink rate across breakpoints than small ones.** A 2.5em headline over 14px mobile body copy computes to 35px, far too big; it wants 20 to 24px there. A button's padding should get proportionally tighter as the button shrinks, not scale with its font size.
239: 5. **ALWAYS add a second signal alongside color.** An icon, a shape or a text cue. For charts, distinguish series by *contrast* — light to dark shades of one color — rather than by hue, because colorblind users read lightness reliably and hue unreliably.
240: 6. **ALWAYS give interactive elements their full state set.** Hover, focus, active and disabled, plus loading and error where they apply. The `:active` state needs a scale transform, or the element feels unresponsive under a finger.
241: 7. **ALWAYS load the matching reference before acting.** `diagnosis-table.md` for an improve task, `review-checklist.md` for a review. Changing UI from a vague complaint without mapping it to a cause is a guess.
242: 
243: ### ❌ NEVER
244: 
245: 1. **NEVER put grey text on a colored background.** Grey on white works because it *reduces contrast*; grey on color just looks dirty. White at reduced opacity looks washed out and disabled, and lets patterns show through the glyphs. Hand-pick a color at the background's hue, adjusting saturation and lightness.
246: 2. **NEVER use `em` for the type scale.** `px` or `rem`. `em` compounds through nesting and silently produces values that are not on the scale. The exception is line length (`max-width` in `em`), where measure should scale with its own text.
247: 3. **NEVER generate shades at runtime** with `lighten()` or `darken()`. Define every shade up front, or the palette drifts into dozens of near-identical colors.
248: 4. **NEVER use a percentage width for something that should not scale.** Sidebars get fixed widths and the main area flexes. Elements get a `max-width` and shrink only when the screen is actually smaller — a login card must not be *wider* at medium screens than at large.
249: 5. **NEVER scale an icon far from its intended size.** A 16 to 24px icon at 48px looks chunky and detail-starved. Put it at its real size inside a colored circle instead.
250: 6. **NEVER remove a focus outline without replacing it.** `outline: none` with no visible replacement is a serious accessibility defect. Replace it with a `box-shadow` ring, which respects border radius.
251: 7. **NEVER animate high-frequency interactions or keyboard navigation.** Focus movement is instant. A search input that animates on every keystroke is a tax paid on every keystroke.
252: 8. **NEVER mix two systems of the same kind in one project** — the five-elevation and two-part shadow scales, or two sets of motion durations. Parallel systems make the thing they encode unreadable.
253: 
254: ### ⚠️ ESCALATE IF
255: 
256: 1. **ESCALATE IF an existing design system or measured Style Reference conflicts with these defaults.** The established system wins. Ask which one governs before overwriting tokens, and say which values would change.
257: 2. **ESCALATE IF a brand color cannot reach 4.5:1 in its required role.** Both escape hatches — flipping to dark colored text on a light tint, and rotating hue toward a brighter one — are in `references/color-system.md`, but changing a brand color is the operator's decision.
258: 3. **ESCALATE IF the request implies a redesign wider than the named surface.** Hierarchy fixes often want to touch competing elements outside the stated scope; name what would need to change and get agreement first.
259: 4. **ESCALATE IF the complaint stays vague after the diagnosis table.** Ask which specific element feels wrong and what it should communicate instead, rather than restyling broadly.
260: 5. **ESCALATE IF a review finds accessibility defects the requester did not ask about.** Report them; do not silently fix code outside the requested scope.
261:

265:

268: - [build-procedure.md](references/build-procedure.md) — the seven-step order of work for something new, and why each step is in that position.

279: 
280: - [tokens.css](assets/tokens.css) — a complete, contrast-verified starting set of every scale above as CSS custom properties, including a semantic role layer and a dark-mode block.
281: - [token-starter-set.md](assets/token-starter-set.md) — what is in `tokens.css`, how to retune it, and the rule that components reference roles rather than raw ramps.

284: 
285: - Load only the references the current intent requires; [`ROUTER.md`](./ROUTER.md) is the routing authority.
286: - The scales themselves stay in this file. They are needed on every invocation, so moving them to a reference would add a load for no benefit.

288: ---

290: ## 6. SUCCESS CRITERIA
291: 
292: ### Task Completion Checklist
293: 
294: **A UI task is complete when:**
295: 
296: - [ ] Every spatial value, font size, weight, shadow, radius and duration came from a scale in Section 3, or from an established system that supersedes it.
297: - [ ] The content has a stated primary, secondary and tertiary tier, separated by weight and color rather than size alone.
298: - [ ] Exactly one primary action is styled as primary on the surface.
299: - [ ] Group spacing exceeds within-group spacing everywhere grouping is meaningful.
300: - [ ] Every text and control pair meets its contrast minimum (4.5:1 normal text, 3:1 large text and functional non-text).
301: - [ ] Interactive elements carry their full state set, and focus is visible.
302: - [ ] Motion durations sit in their band, similar elements share values, and nothing animates that should not.
303: - [ ] No hard rule in Section 4 is violated, or each deviation is stated with its reason.
304: 
305: ### Quality Gates
306: 
307: - **Scale conformance**: zero off-scale values, or each one named and justified.
308: - **Color count**: shades come from a defined ramp; no runtime-generated shades.
309: - **Breakpoint behavior**: large elements shrink faster than small ones; nothing scales proportionally.
310: - **Signal redundancy**: no state or category communicated by color alone.
311: - **Review output**: every finding carries a file, a line, a fix, and a criterion where one applies.
312: 
313: ---
314: 
315: ## 7. INTEGRATION POINTS
316: 
317: ### Inputs
318: 
319: - The surface in scope: a component, a screen, a described complaint, or a set of files to review.
320: - Optionally, an existing token file, design system, or a measured `DESIGN.md` Style Reference. Any of these **outranks** this skill's defaults.
321: 
322: ### Outputs
323: 
324: - Concrete values and CSS, plus the reason each value was chosen from its scale.
325: - For an improve task, the symptom-to-cause mapping that justified each change.
326: - For a review, severity-tiered findings with file, line and fix.
327: 
328: ### Related Workflows
329: 
330: - **`sk-design-md-generator`** measures a live site's real CSS into a v3 Style Reference. It is the reading half of the pair; this skill is the writing half. When a Style Reference exists for the surface, its measured values are ground truth and this skill supplies only what the reference left undecided.
331: - **`sk-code`** implements the result. Hand it the chosen values, not adjectives.
332: - **`system-spec-kit`** owns packet documentation and continuity when the work is tracked.
333: 
334: ### Reading Versus Authoring
335: 
336: `sk-design-md-generator/references/design-knowledge/numeric-design-laws.md` records type ratios, spacing and motion bands for *reading* a measured surface. This skill decides them for a surface not yet built. A measurement outranks a default, and [`references/motion-principles.md`](references/motion-principles.md) Section 5 states the reconciliation.
337: 
338: ---
339: 
340: ## 8. REFERENCES AND RELATED RESOURCES
341: 
342: [`ROUTER.md`](./ROUTER.md) governs what loads. This skill ships no scripts: every decision is a judgment, not an automated transform. Related skills are named in Section 7.
343: 
344: ### Sources
345: 
346: Original notes derived from four public sources, captured 2026-08-28. None of their text is reproduced verbatim.

7: 
8: # Visual Design
9: 
10: Visual design is not talent. It is a small set of systems decisions made **once**, plus a handful of
11: techniques for building hierarchy, a set of interaction details that make a screen behave correctly,
12: and a motion model that keeps it feeling human.
13: 
14: **Most of that is not about screens.** A spacing scale, a type scale, a colour ramp and a hierarchy
15: pyramid decide a slide, a printed page and a report layout as much as they decide a component. The
16: sections below say which parts carry to every surface and which are genuinely screen-only, so a deck
17: question gets the systems and skips the focus rings.
18: 
19: The single biggest cause of amateur-looking UI is picking values ad hoc — 17px here, `#3B82F6` there, `lighten(5%)` for a hover state, `400ms` because it seemed smooth. Design *from a scale*, always.
20: 
21: > **Boundary.** This skill decides values and behavior when UI is being **built, fixed, or reviewed**. It is prescriptive and emits CSS. It does not measure an existing site — `sk-design-md-generator` extracts a live surface's real CSS into a measured Style Reference, and when such a reference exists its measured values win over the defaults here. See Section 7.
22: 
23: ---
24: 
25: ## 1. WHEN TO USE
26: 
27: ### Activation Triggers
28: 
29: **Use when** the task involves:
30: - Building or styling any interface — web page, app screen, dashboard, landing page, single component.
31: - Picking a concrete value: font size, spacing, padding, color, shadow, border radius, border width, opacity, duration.
32: - Designing a color palette, a shade ramp, or a set of design tokens from scratch.
33: - Implementing inputs, menus, tooltips, dialogs, or anything with focus, keyboard and touch behavior.
34: - Adding or tuning animation, or deciding whether something should animate at all.
35: - Reviewing UI code for accessibility and visual quality, with findings rather than impressions.
36: - Improving UI that already exists, especially against a vague complaint.
37: 
38: **Keyword Triggers**: the routing vocabulary is the keyword comment above the title; it is the single list, so it is not restated here.
39: 
40: ### Use Cases
41: 
42: - **Building new UI.** The systems in Section 3 replace every ad hoc value decision; the interaction and motion references cover the behavior the values do not.
43: - **Improving existing UI.** A vague complaint maps to a small number of mechanical causes. The symptom-to-fix table is the entry point.
44: - **Reviewing UI code.** A severity-tiered pass over real files: WCAG-cited accessibility first, then visual, component and motion checks, each finding carrying a file, a line and a fix.
45: 
46: ### When NOT to Use
47: 
48: **Skip this skill when**:
49: - The task is measuring or documenting a **live site's** existing CSS. That is extraction, and it belongs to `sk-design-md-generator`.
50: - A measured Style Reference or an established design system already fixes the values. Those are ground truth; this skill's defaults are for what nobody has decided yet.
51: - The work is application logic, state or data flow with no visual or interaction surface. Route to `sk-code`.
52: - The request is brand identity, logo design, illustration, or copywriting.
53:

55: 
56: ## 2. SMART ROUTING
57: 
58: The `sk-design` hub routes a design request here when it decides a value or judges a surface against values, and the hub's `VALUES` and `REVIEW` intents select this packet.
59: A request that measures a live surface belongs to `sk-design-md-generator`; this packet supplies only the defaults a measurement outranks.
60: The request is **build**, **improve** or **review**, and that split decides which reference loads first.
61: The scales and hard rules in this file load on every invocation.
62: An improve task loads `references/diagnosis-table.md` first, a review loads `references/review-checklist.md`, and something new loads `references/build-procedure.md`.
63: A request naming one property needs only its scale; *"make this look designed"* also needs the hierarchy technique in Section 3.
64: The two assets load only on explicit request.
65: 
66: Read [`ROUTER.md`](./ROUTER.md) before selecting skill-local resources; open only the matched files.
