69: 
70: ## 3. HOW IT WORKS
71: 
72: ### The Surfaces
73: 
74: The systems below are surface-agnostic. What differs is which of the extras apply.
75: 
76: | Surface | Systems that apply | What changes | What does not apply |
77: | --- | --- | --- | --- |
78: | **Screen UI** | All four | The reference surface these rules were written against | Nothing |
79: | **Slide decks** | All four | Far fewer elements per view, so hierarchy does more work and the type scale runs larger. Transitions replace interaction motion | Focus rings, hover, touch targets |
80: | **Printed layouts** | All four | No dark mode and no hover state. Contrast still matters and is harder, because paper has no backlight. Measure in a physical unit and keep the spacing ratios | Interaction craft, motion, response budgets |
81: | **Document layouts** | All four | Reading order is the hierarchy. Long-form type scale runs tighter than UI, and white space carries the structure | Interaction craft, motion |
82: | **Chart and diagram canvases** | Colour and type scale only | Those canvases have their own layout rules | Everything else; the canvas modes own it |
83: 
84: Two references are screen-only: [`interaction-craft.md`](references/interaction-craft.md) and
85: [`motion-principles.md`](references/motion-principles.md). A deck may borrow the motion timings for
86: transitions; a printed page has no use for either. Everything else in `references/` applies whatever
87: the surface.
88: 
89: ### The Systems
90: 
91: Pick from these lists. Never invent a value that is not on one.
92: 
93: #### Spacing and sizing
94: 
95: Base 16px, built from factors and multiples of it:
96: 
97: ```text
98: 4  8  12  16  24  32  48  64  96  128  192  256  384  512  640  768
99: ```
100: 
101: Tight at the small end, spreading out at the large end. **No two adjacent values may be closer than about 25%** — that is what makes the choice obvious. A linear "multiples of 4" scale fails, because it does not help anyone decide between 120px and 124px.
102: 
103: Use it for margin, padding, width, height, icon sizes and border width — everything spatial. Fix a small set of opacity values too (`.05 .1 .2 .4 .6 .8`) for disabled states, overlays and hover tints, rather than eyeballing a slider each time. Same logic as the other scales: decide once, reuse everywhere.
104: 
105: #### Type scale
106: 
107: ```text
108: 12  14  16  18  20  24  30  36  48  60  72
109: ```
110: 
111: Not a modular scale built from a ratio. Ratios produce fractional pixel values that round inconsistently across browsers, and they are too sparse for interface density. Hand-picked values, chosen for how they feel, win instead.
112: 
113: **Units: `px` or `rem` only. Never `em`.** `em` is relative to the current font size, so `.875em` inside a `1.25em` parent computes to 17.5px — a value not on the scale. The scale silently stops existing.
114: 
115: #### Font weight
116: 
117: Two weights is enough:
118: 
119: - **400 or 500** for body and most UI text.
120: - **600 or 700** for anything emphasized. Medium-sized headings usually sit best at 500 to 600.
121: 
122: Nothing below 400 in UI. To de-emphasize, use a lighter *color* or a smaller *size*, never a lighter weight. Weight must also not change on hover or selection, because the width change shifts the layout.
123: 
124: #### Color
125: 
126: A five-swatch palette generator gives nowhere near enough colors.
127: 
128: - **Greys: 8 to 10 shades.** Almost all of a UI is grey — text, backgrounds, panels, borders, form controls. Three or four shades always runs out. Start at a very dark grey, not true black, which looks unnatural.
129: - **Primary: 5 to 10 shades**, one or at most two primaries.
130: - **Accents: 5 to 10 shades each** — destructive red, warning yellow, positive green, plus whatever else the product must distinguish. Ten colors at 5 to 10 shades each is normal for a complex UI.
131: 
132: Name them `100` (lightest) through `900` (darkest), base `500`.
133: 
134: **Build the ramp in one order:** base `500` first, then the `900` and `100` edges, then the gap fills — the reasoning, and the button-background test that decides `500`, are in [`references/color-system.md`](references/color-system.md) Section 3.
135: 
136: **Write colors as HSL, not hex.** `hsl(220, 95%, 34%)` and `hsl(220, 65%, 61%)` are visibly related; `#03369E` and `#507DD7` are not.
137: 
138: **Never generate shades at runtime** with `lighten()` or `darken()`. That is how a project ends up with 35 slightly different blues.
139: 
140: Full construction method — base selection, saturation at the ends, hue rotation, dark mode, contrast escape hatches — is in [`references/color-system.md`](references/color-system.md).
141: 
142: #### Shadows, five elevations
143: 
144: ```css
145: 0 1px 3px   hsla(0,0%,0%,.2)   /* barely raised - buttons */
146: 0 4px 6px   hsla(0,0%,0%,.2)   /* dropdowns */
147: 0 5px 15px  hsla(0,0%,0%,.2)
148: 0 10px 24px hsla(0,0%,0%,.2)
149: 0 15px 35px hsla(0,0%,0%,.2)   /* modals */
150: ```
151: 
152: Choose by asking *where on the z-axis does this sit?*, not *what shadow looks nice?*. Closer to the user means more attention. Shrinking a button's shadow on `:active` makes it feel pressed. Growing a list item's shadow when it is picked up for drag-to-reorder does the reverse — it reads as "now above its siblings" and doubles as the drag affordance.
153: 
154: Every shadow in a project shares one offset direction, because there is one light source. [`references/depth-and-detail.md`](references/depth-and-detail.md) carries two refined alternatives:
155: 
156: - a **two-part** cast-plus-contact scale
157: - a **layered** three-part set
158: 
159: It also carries the rule for tinting shadow color on non-white surfaces, and the full six-layer button anatomy. The three systems are parallel and not compatible. Pick one per project and never mix them, or elevation stops being readable.
160: 
161: #### Line-height and line length
162: 
163: Line-height is **inversely** proportional to font size, and proportional to line width:
164: 
165: - small text or wide columns: `1.5` to `2`
166: - large headlines: `1` is fine
167: 
168: Line length: **45 to 75 characters**, which is `max-width: 20em` to `35em`. This applies to the paragraph even when its container is wider. Mixed widths in one content area look more polished, not less.
169: 
170: `em` is correct *here* — measure should scale with the text it wraps. The "never `em`" rule is scoped to the *type scale*, where `em` compounds through nesting. Do not "fix" this.
171: 
172: #### Border radius
173: 
174: Pick one and stay consistent. Small radius reads neutral, large reads playful, none reads serious or formal. Mixing square and rounded corners in one interface always looks worse. For nested elements, inner radius equals outer radius minus the padding between them.
175: 
176: #### Motion durations
177: 
178: Timing is a scale like the others, and consistency across it outranks the perfect value for any one element.
179: 
180: ```text
181: 120-180ms   press, hover, direct feedback
182: 180-260ms   small state change: toggle, dropdown, tooltip, tab
183: up to 500ms layout transition: modal, drawer, accordion
184: ```
185: 
186: 300ms is the ceiling for anything the user initiated. Similar elements use identical values. The full model — easing curves, springs, staging, and when not to animate at all — is in [`references/motion-principles.md`](references/motion-principles.md).
187: 
188: ### The Procedure
189: 
190: Seven steps govern the order of work on something new: start from a feature rather than a layout, work in **grayscale first**, treat low-fidelity artifacts as disposable, build the smallest useful version, **choose each value by elimination** against its two neighbours on the scale, start with too much white space and trim, and design at about 400px before relaxing to a large screen.
191: 
192: Full steps with their reasoning: [`references/build-procedure.md`](references/build-procedure.md). Load it when starting something new; a value question does not need it.
193: 
194: ### Hierarchy, The Technique That Does The Most Work
195: 
196: Everything on the surface sits in a pyramid: primary, secondary, tertiary. When everything competes, the surface reads as noise. This is the most surface-agnostic technique here: a slide with three competing headings fails the same way a screen does. This is what makes a design look designed, not styling.
197: 
198: Four rules carry most of it:
199: 
200: - **size is not everything**: weight and color carry the emphasis, with sizes kept near the middle of the scale
201: - **three text colors, maximum**: all three at 4.5:1
202: - **emphasize by de-emphasizing**: soften the competition rather than amplifying the primary
203: - **style actions by hierarchy, not by semantics**
204: 
205: The full method is in [`references/hierarchy.md`](references/hierarchy.md) Sections 2 through 7. It covers the destructive-action treatment, label suppression, the weight-versus-contrast trade, and why visual hierarchy may disagree with document hierarchy.
206: 
207: ### Beyond The Visual System
208: 
209: Correct values do not make a screen behave correctly. Six references carry the behavior, each on its own intent:
210: 
211: - [`build-procedure.md`](references/build-procedure.md) Section 2
212: - [`hierarchy.md`](references/hierarchy.md) Sections 1 and 3
213: - [`interaction-craft.md`](references/interaction-craft.md) Sections 3 and 5
214: - [`motion-principles.md`](references/motion-principles.md) Section 4
215: - [`ux-laws.md`](references/ux-laws.md) Sections 2 to 5
216: - [`review-checklist.md`](references/review-checklist.md) Sections 2 to 6
217: 
218: ### Project Profile Slot
219: 
220: A project may add an optional `references/<project>-profile.md` holding its own values. A profile loads only when the request names that project's UI. An unknown or unnamed project loads none, and the slot adds no routing phrase, since naming the project is what reaches it. When sources disagree, the order is:
221: 
222: 1. The repository's mode.
223: 2. The tokens the app installs.
224: 3. The design scales in this file.
225: 4. The profile.
226: 
227: ---
228: 
229: ## 4. RULES
230: 
231: ### ✅ ALWAYS
232: 
233: 1. **ALWAYS pick values from the scales in Section 3.** A value off the scale is the defect this skill exists to prevent; it is what makes a UI read as amateur even when nothing is individually wrong. Timing is a scale too.
234: 2. **ALWAYS put more space around a group than within it.** This is the fix for "which label belongs to which field", cramped bullet lists (the gap must exceed the line-height), and headings that look attached to the wrong paragraph. Ambiguous spacing is a functional bug, not only an ugly one.

236:     - **3:1 applies to non-text** (WCAG 1.4.11). A border that is the only thing identifying a control, such as an input outline or a checkbox edge, needs 3:1 against its background.
237:     - A hairline that merely divides content does not. Text and non-text are two different tokens.

239: 5. **ALWAYS add a second signal alongside color.** An icon, a shape or a text cue. For charts, distinguish series by *contrast* — light to dark shades of one color — rather than by hue, because colorblind users read lightness reliably and hue unreliably.
240: 6. **ALWAYS give interactive elements their full state set.** Hover, focus, active and disabled, plus loading and error where they apply. The `:active` state needs a scale transform, or the element feels unresponsive under a finger.
241: 7. **ALWAYS load the matching reference before acting.** `diagnosis-table.md` for an improve task, `review-checklist.md` for a review. Changing UI from a vague complaint without mapping it to a cause is a guess.
242: 
243: ### ❌ NEVER
244: 
245: 1. **NEVER put grey text on a colored background.** Grey on white works because it *reduces contrast*; grey on color just looks dirty. White at reduced opacity looks washed out and disabled, and lets patterns show through the glyphs. Hand-pick a color at the background's hue, adjusting saturation and lightness.
246: 2. **NEVER use `em` for the type scale.** `px` or `rem`. `em` compounds through nesting and silently produces values that are not on the scale. The exception is line length (`max-width` in `em`), where measure should scale with its own text.
247: 3. **NEVER generate shades at runtime** with `lighten()` or `darken()`. Define every shade up front, or the palette drifts into dozens of near-identical colors.
248: 4. **NEVER use a percentage width for something that should not scale.** Sidebars get fixed widths and the main area flexes. Elements get a `max-width` and shrink only when the screen is actually smaller — a login card must not be *wider* at medium screens than at large.
249: 5. **NEVER scale an icon far from its intended size.** A 16 to 24px icon at 48px looks chunky and detail-starved. Put it at its real size inside a colored circle instead.
250: 6. **NEVER remove a focus outline without replacing it.** `outline: none` with no visible replacement is a serious accessibility defect. Replace it with a `box-shadow` ring, which respects border radius.
251: 7. **NEVER animate high-frequency interactions or keyboard navigation.** Focus movement is instant. A search input that animates on every keystroke is a tax paid on every keystroke.
252: 8. **NEVER mix two systems of the same kind in one project** — the five-elevation and two-part shadow scales, or two sets of motion durations. Parallel systems make the thing they encode unreadable.
253:

255: 
256: 1. **ESCALATE IF an existing design system or measured Style Reference conflicts with these defaults.** The established system wins. Ask which one governs before overwriting tokens, and say which values would change.
257: 2. **ESCALATE IF a brand color cannot reach 4.5:1 in its required role.** Both escape hatches — flipping to dark colored text on a light tint, and rotating hue toward a brighter one — are in `references/color-system.md`, but changing a brand color is the operator's decision.
258: 3. **ESCALATE IF the request implies a redesign wider than the named surface.** Hierarchy fixes often want to touch competing elements outside the stated scope; name what would need to change and get agreement first.
259: 4. **ESCALATE IF the complaint stays vague after the diagnosis table.** Ask which specific element feels wrong and what it should communicate instead, rather than restyling broadly.

14: # Token Starter Set
15: 
16: `tokens.css` is a complete, contrast-verified expression of every scale in this skill, ready to copy into a project and retune.
17: 
18: ---
19: 
20: ## 1. OVERVIEW
21: 
22: ### Core Principle
23: 
24: Copy it in and retune the hues. Re-deriving the scales from prose wastes the work already done and reintroduces the ad hoc values the system exists to eliminate.
25: 
26: ### When to Use
27: 
28: - Starting a project with no established design system.
29: - Adding a token layer to a codebase that currently hardcodes values.
30: - Needing a worked example of a ramp that already satisfies the saturation and contrast rules.
31: 
32: ### What It Is Not
33: 
34: It is not a theme, a component library, or a brand. It is the decisions, made once, with the hues chosen to be replaced.
35: 
36: ---
37: 
38: ## 2. WHAT IS IN THE FILE
39: 
40: | Group | Tokens | Notes |
41: |---|---|---|
42: | Spacing and sizing | `--space-1` through `--space-16` | 4px to 768px, no two neighbours closer than about 25% |
43: | Type scale | `--text-xs` through `--text-7xl` | 12px to 72px, `px` values |
44: | Weight | `--weight-normal`, `--weight-bold` | 400 and 600; nothing below 400 exists |
45: | Line-height and measure | `--leading-tight` to `--leading-loose`, `--measure` | `--measure: 34em` keeps lines at 45 to 75 characters |
46: | Greys | `--grey-100` through `--grey-900` | Cool-tinted, hue about 209 to 212. Each carries its measured contrast ratio in a comment |
47: | Primary | `--primary-100` through `--primary-900` | Nine shades; `500` is the button-background shade |
48: | Accents | `red`, `yellow`, `green` at `100`, `500`, `800` | The trio that "flip the contrast" needs: tint, solid fill, text on the tint |
49: | Elevation | `--shadow-1` through `--shadow-5` | The five-elevation scale, with heavier alphas in dark mode |
50: | Radius | `--radius`, `--radius-full` | 4px neutral default |
51: | Border width | `--border-width`, `--border-width-thick` | 1px and 2px, for the "keep the soft color, go to 2px" fix |
52: | Opacity | `--opacity-1` through `--opacity-6` | `.05` to `.8`, so overlays stop being eyeballed |
53: | Semantic roles | `--surface`, `--text-primary`, `--action`, and the rest | The layer components actually reference |
54: 
55: ---
56: 
57: ## 3. THE ROLE LAYER
58: 
59: **Reference the roles in components, not the raw ramps.** This is what makes the dark-mode block work: the dark override redefines only the roles, so every component that points at `--text-secondary` follows automatically, while a component pointing at `--grey-700` does not.
60: 
61: ```css
62: /* Right - follows the mode */
63: .card { background: var(--surface-raised); color: var(--text-primary); }
64: 
65: /* Wrong - locked to light mode */
66: .card { background: #fff; color: var(--grey-900); }
67: ```
68: 
69: Two roles are deliberately distinct and are the pair most often collapsed by mistake:
70: 
71: - `--border` is **decorative** — dividers and separators, about 1.3:1. It has no contrast obligation.
72: - `--border-strong` is **functional** — input outlines, checkbox edges, focus rings. Anything that is the only thing identifying a control needs 3:1 against its background under WCAG 1.4.11.
73: 
74: Collapsing them into one token either makes dividers too loud or makes controls unidentifiable.
75: 
76: ---
77: 
78: ## 4. WHICH GREY FOR WHICH TEXT
79: 
80: The grey ramp is not interchangeable. Each step has a verified role.
81: 
82: | Token | Ratio vs `--grey-100` | Use for |
83: |---|---|---|
84: | `--grey-400` | 2.7:1 | Disabled text only. WCAG exempts inactive components — it does **not** exempt placeholders, which are active content |
85: | `--grey-500` | 3.9:1 | Large text only: 24px regular or 18.66px bold. Not safe for a 12px eyebrow label |
86: | `--grey-600` | 5.6:1 | Tertiary text — footnotes, copyright |
87: | `--grey-700` | 8.0:1 | Secondary text |
88: | `--grey-900` | 13.4:1 | Primary text |
89: 
90: On pure white each ratio is about 10% higher than the figure above.
91: 
92: The "three text colors, maximum" rule in `SKILL.md` maps to `--text-primary`, `--text-secondary` and `--text-tertiary`. All three carry body-size text, so all three clear 4.5:1 — which is why tertiary is `--grey-600` and not something paler.
93: 
94: ---
95: 
96: ## 5. RETUNING FOR A PROJECT
97: 
98: 1. **Change the primary hue first.** Rotate all nine `--primary-*` shades together and keep their lightness and saturation relationships intact.
99: 2. **Re-check the base.** `--primary-500` must still work as a button background with white text. Different hues need different lightness to do that, so verify rather than assuming the rotation preserved it.
100: 3. **Decide grey temperature.** The file ships cool greys at hue 209 to 212. For warm greys, move the hue to about 39 to 41 and keep the saturation pattern.
101: 4. **Keep saturation rising toward the ends.** If a shade gets edited, the palest and darkest steps must stay *more* saturated than the base, or they drift toward neutral.
102: 5. **Expand accents only when used heavily.** The `100/500/800` trio covers pills, badges and alerts. A full nine-shade ramp is worth building only when a color carries a real surface.
103: 6. **Re-verify every text and surface pair after retuning.** The shipped ratios are measured against the shipped values; a hue rotation changes them.
104: 
105: The deliberate sub-threshold values — disabled text, decorative dividers, the large-text-only step — are exempt by criterion and are commented inline in the file. Keep the comments when copying; they are why the next person does not "fix" a value that is correct.
106: 
107: ---
108: 
109: ## 6. REFERENCES AND RELATED RESOURCES
110: 
111: - [`tokens.css`](tokens.css) — the file itself.
112: - [`../references/color-system.md`](../references/color-system.md) — the construction method behind these ramps, and what to do when a brand color cannot reach its ratio.
113: - [`../references/depth-and-detail.md`](../references/depth-and-detail.md) Section 3 — the two-part shadow alternative to `--shadow-1` through `--shadow-5`, for designs where shadows are prominent.

14: 
15: # Build Procedure
16: 
17: Seven steps for designing something that does not exist yet. They govern the order of work, not the values — the scales in `SKILL.md` decide those.
18: 
19: ---
20: 
21: ## 1. OVERVIEW
22: 
23: ### Core Principle
24: 
25: Most bad interfaces come from designing in the wrong order: the shell before the feature, color before hierarchy, the desktop before the phone. Fixing the order removes most of the work.
26: 
27: ### When to Use
28: 
29: - Starting a screen, page or component from nothing.
30: - Stuck on a layout decision that will not resolve.
31: - Deciding how much white space something needs.
32: - Choosing between two adjacent values on a scale.
33: 
34: ### When Not to Use
35: 
36: Improving something that exists already. That is [`diagnosis-table.md`](diagnosis-table.md), which starts from the complaint instead.
37: 
38: ---
39: 
40: ## 2. THE SEVEN STEPS
41: 
42: ### 1. Start with a feature, not a layout
43: 
44: Nobody can choose between a top nav and a sidebar before knowing what is in the product. Design one real piece of functionality — the search form, the message composer, the row of a list — and let the shell emerge from what the features turn out to need.
45: 
46: Designing the shell first produces a shell that the features then have to fit into, which is backwards and shows.
47: 
48: ### 2. Detail comes later
49: 
50: Work in **grayscale first**. Removing color forces hierarchy to come from spacing, contrast and size, which are the things that actually carry it. A layout that reads correctly in grayscale reads correctly in color; the reverse is not true, because color can prop up a hierarchy that does not exist.
51: 
52: Typefaces, shadows and icons wait until the layout works.
53: 
54: ### 3. Do not over-invest in low fidelity
55: 
56: Sketches, wireframes and mockups are disposable. Nobody can use a static picture of an app, so their only job is to explore ideas cheaply. Once the decision is made, abandon them and build the real thing rather than polishing an artifact that will be thrown away.
57: 
58: ### 4. Design the smallest useful version, then build it
59: 
60: Work in short design-to-code cycles. The screen in a browser tells the truth; the mockup does not.
61: 
62: Do not imply functionality that is not ready to build. A comment box with an attachments zone that cannot ship yet blocks the whole feature — either build the attachment or remove its affordance.
63: 
64: ### 5. Choose by elimination
65: 
66: When picking a value from a scale, do not evaluate it in isolation. Guess the step that seems right, then compare it against the neighbour on each side. Two of the three will be obviously wrong, which makes the decision fast and repeatable.
67: 
68: If an outer option wins, re-run the comparison with that as the new middle. Stop when the middle wins.
69: 
70: This works because a constrained scale makes adjacent values distinguishable. It is also why the spacing scale keeps neighbours about 25% apart: on a linear scale the comparison is meaningless.
71: 
72: ### 6. Start with too much white space and remove it
73: 
74: Adding space until something stops looking bad gives the **minimum** acceptable amount. Starting generous and trimming gives the **right** amount. The two rarely land in the same place.
75: 
76: Dense interfaces such as dashboards and data tables are legitimate, but as a deliberate decision made once, not as the default that emerges from never having had enough space to begin with.
77: 
78: ### 7. Shrink the canvas
79: 
80: A small component designed on a 1400px artboard sprawls, because the space is there to fill. Start at about 400px and design the mobile layout first, where the constraints are real and every element has to earn its space.
81: 
82: Then bring it to a large screen and relax only what genuinely felt cramped. That is less than expected, and the discipline survives into the desktop layout.
83: 
84: ---
85: 
86: ## 3. WHAT THE PROCEDURE DOES NOT DECIDE
87:

90: - Spacing, type, weight, color, elevation, radius, opacity and duration are in `SKILL.md` Section 3.

92: - Hierarchy technique is in [`hierarchy.md`](hierarchy.md), and it is what step 2's grayscale pass is testing.

94: A procedure followed with invented values produces the same amateur result in a better order.

14: 
15: # Build Procedure
16: 
17: Seven steps for designing something that does not exist yet. They govern the order of work, not the values — the scales in `SKILL.md` decide those.
18: 
19: ---
20: 
21: ## 1. OVERVIEW
22: 
23: ### Core Principle
24: 
25: Most bad interfaces come from designing in the wrong order: the shell before the feature, color before hierarchy, the desktop before the phone. Fixing the order removes most of the work.
26: 
27: ### When to Use
28: 
29: - Starting a screen, page or component from nothing.
30: - Stuck on a layout decision that will not resolve.
31: - Deciding how much white space something needs.
32: - Choosing between two adjacent values on a scale.
33: 
34: ### When Not to Use
35: 
36: Improving something that exists already. That is [`diagnosis-table.md`](diagnosis-table.md), which starts from the complaint instead.
37: 
38: ---
39: 
40: ## 2. THE SEVEN STEPS
41: 
42: ### 1. Start with a feature, not a layout
43: 
44: Nobody can choose between a top nav and a sidebar before knowing what is in the product. Design one real piece of functionality — the search form, the message composer, the row of a list — and let the shell emerge from what the features turn out to need.
45: 
46: Designing the shell first produces a shell that the features then have to fit into, which is backwards and shows.
47: 
48: ### 2. Detail comes later
49: 
50: Work in **grayscale first**. Removing color forces hierarchy to come from spacing, contrast and size, which are the things that actually carry it. A layout that reads correctly in grayscale reads correctly in color; the reverse is not true, because color can prop up a hierarchy that does not exist.
51: 
52: Typefaces, shadows and icons wait until the layout works.
53: 
54: ### 3. Do not over-invest in low fidelity
55: 
56: Sketches, wireframes and mockups are disposable. Nobody can use a static picture of an app, so their only job is to explore ideas cheaply. Once the decision is made, abandon them and build the real thing rather than polishing an artifact that will be thrown away.
57: 
58: ### 4. Design the smallest useful version, then build it
59: 
60: Work in short design-to-code cycles. The screen in a browser tells the truth; the mockup does not.
61: 
62: Do not imply functionality that is not ready to build. A comment box with an attachments zone that cannot ship yet blocks the whole feature — either build the attachment or remove its affordance.
63: 
64: ### 5. Choose by elimination
65: 
66: When picking a value from a scale, do not evaluate it in isolation. Guess the step that seems right, then compare it against the neighbour on each side. Two of the three will be obviously wrong, which makes the decision fast and repeatable.
67: 
68: If an outer option wins, re-run the comparison with that as the new middle. Stop when the middle wins.
69: 
70: This works because a constrained scale makes adjacent values distinguishable. It is also why the spacing scale keeps neighbours about 25% apart: on a linear scale the comparison is meaningless.
71: 
72: ### 6. Start with too much white space and remove it
73: 
74: Adding space until something stops looking bad gives the **minimum** acceptable amount. Starting generous and trimming gives the **right** amount. The two rarely land in the same place.
75: 
76: Dense interfaces such as dashboards and data tables are legitimate, but as a deliberate decision made once, not as the default that emerges from never having had enough space to begin with.
77: 
78: ### 7. Shrink the canvas
79: 
80: A small component designed on a 1400px artboard sprawls, because the space is there to fill. Start at about 400px and design the mobile layout first, where the constraints are real and every element has to earn its space.
81: 
82: Then bring it to a large screen and relax only what genuinely felt cramped. That is less than expected, and the discipline survives into the desktop layout.
83: 
84: ---
85: 
86: ## 3. WHAT THE PROCEDURE DOES NOT DECIDE
87: 
88: The steps govern order and process. Every actual value still comes from a scale:
89: 
90: - Spacing, type, weight, color, elevation, radius, opacity and duration are in `SKILL.md` Section 3.
91: - Palette construction is in [`color-system.md`](color-system.md).
92: - Hierarchy technique is in [`hierarchy.md`](hierarchy.md), and it is what step 2's grayscale pass is testing.
93: 
94: A procedure followed with invented values produces the same amateur result in a better order.
95: 
96: ---
97: 
98: ## 4. REFERENCES AND RELATED RESOURCES
99: 
100: - [`diagnosis-table.md`](diagnosis-table.md) — the counterpart for surfaces that already exist.
101: - [`ux-laws.md`](ux-laws.md) — the cognitive constraints that explain why several of these steps work.
102: - [`color-system.md`](color-system.md) — where step 2's deferred color decision gets made.

14: 
15: # Depth and Detail Techniques
16: 
17: The techniques that turn a correctly-scaled layout into something that looks finished: light, shadow, alignment, type detail, and images.
18: 
19: ---
20: 
21: ## 1. OVERVIEW
22: 
23: ### Core Principle
24: 
25: Borrow the real-world cue and stop. Depth comes from mimicking one light source consistently, not from chasing photorealism.
26: 
27: ### When to Use
28: 
29: - An element needs to read as raised, inset, or pressed.
30: - Shadows are prominent in the design and the five-elevation default is not enough.
31: - Typography looks subtly wrong at the detail level: mixed sizes on a line, all-caps labels, headline tracking.
32: - A component looks generic and nobody can say why.
33: - Images, screenshots, icons or user-uploaded content are breaking the layout.
34: 
35: ### Prerequisites
36: 
37: The default five-elevation shadow scale is in `SKILL.md` Section 3. Section 3 of this document gives the refined two-part alternative. The two are parallel systems — never mix them in one project.
38: 
39: ---
40: 
41: ## 2. EMULATING A LIGHT SOURCE
42: 
43: Raised and inset are the same trick: decide the element's **profile**, then mimic how light would hit that shape. Light comes from above, and people look slightly *down* at their screens, so the top edge of a raised element is visible and the bottom edge of an inset one is.
44: 
45: Each element needs **both** effects — the lit edge and the blocked light. They go in a single comma-separated `box-shadow`. Two `box-shadow` declarations on one selector do not combine; the second silently discards the first.
46: 
47: **Raised**, for a button or card: lit top edge, shadow cast below.
48: 
49: ```css
50: box-shadow:
51:   inset 0 1px 0 hsl(224, 84%, 74%),   /* top edge, angled toward the light */
52:   0 1px 3px hsla(0, 0%, 0%, .2);      /* light blocked beneath the element */
53: ```
54: 
55: **Inset**, for a well, text input or checkbox: lit bottom lip, shadow blocked at the top. The lip must be **lighter than the element's own face**, so the values depend entirely on how dark that face is.
56: 
57: ```css
58: /* Dark surface - the face is dark, so the lip has room to read as clearly lit. */
59: box-shadow:
60:   inset 0 -2px 0 hsl(211, 30%, 34%),    /* bottom lip, on a grey-800 face */
61:   inset 0 2px 2px hsla(0, 0%, 0%, .25); /* light blocked by the lip above */
62: 
63: /* Light surface - the face is already near-white, so there is almost no room to
64:    go lighter. Let the top shadow do the work and keep the lip to a hairline. */
65: box-shadow:
66:   inset 0 -1px 0 hsl(0, 0%, 100%),      /* on a grey-100 face */
67:   inset 0 2px 2px hsla(0, 0%, 0%, .06);
68: ```
69: 
70: Copying dark-surface values onto a white input paints a dark line along the bottom, which reads as a stray border — the opposite of the intended cue. Always check the lip against the face.
71: 
72: Both lit edges are `inset`. A non-inset shadow with a negative Y offset draws *above* the element, not on its bottom lip.
73: 
74: Two rules govern the lit edge:
75: 
76: - **Hand-pick the lighter color** rather than overlaying semi-transparent white. White overlays drain the saturation out of the underlying color, which is why both examples above use a solid `hsl()` sampled from the element's own hue. On a neutral grey or near-black surface there is no saturation to lose, so `hsla(0,0%,100%,.15)` is fine there.
77: - **Keep blur radii tiny.** These edges are sharp in the real world, like the shadow under a wall outlet.
78: 
79: ---
80: 
81: ## 3. TWO-PART SHADOWS
82: 
83: Good shadows are usually two shadows doing two different jobs.
84: 
85: - **Cast shadow**: larger and softer, bigger Y offset and blur. The shadow thrown behind the object by direct light.
86: - **Contact shadow**: tighter, small offset and blur. The area *underneath* the object that even ambient light cannot reach. This is what keeps the element's edges defined.
87: 
88: ```css
89: box-shadow:
90:   0 10px 20px hsla(0, 0%, 0%, .15),  /* cast    - larger, softer */
91:   0 3px 6px   hsla(0, 0%, 0%, .10);  /* contact - tighter, sharper */
92: ```
93: 
94: The two parts must differ *substantially* in offset and blur or the effect is invisible — about a threefold difference in both, as above.
95: 
96: **Which one is darker depends on elevation, and that is the whole point.** At rest on the surface the contact shadow is the darker of the two (`.24` against the cast shadow's `.12`). As the object lifts, the contact shadow fades out and ends up lighter, until at the top of the scale it is gone entirely. Do not fix the alphas; let them cross over. Keep both inside `.05` to `.25`, because anything heavier reads as a smudge.
97: 
98: ```css
99: /* lowest  */ 0 1px 3px hsla(0,0%,0%,.12), 0 1px 2px hsla(0,0%,0%,.24);
100: /*         */ 0 3px 6px hsla(0,0%,0%,.15), 0 2px 4px hsla(0,0%,0%,.12);
101: /*         */ 0 10px 20px hsla(0,0%,0%,.15), 0 3px 6px hsla(0,0%,0%,.10);
102: /*         */ 0 15px 25px hsla(0,0%,0%,.15), 0 5px 10px hsla(0,0%,0%,.05);
103: /* highest */ 0 20px 40px hsla(0,0%,0%,.2);
104: ```
105: 
106: Distinct at the lowest elevation, gone entirely at the highest — lift an object off a desk and the dark contact shadow disappears first.
107: 
108: The tradeoff: at the lowest elevations the two shadows converge in geometry (`0 1px 3px` plus `0 1px 2px`) and the technique buys little beyond a slightly crisper edge. That is why the plain five-elevation scale in `SKILL.md` remains the default when shadows are not prominent in the design.
109: 
110: ### Three parallel systems, pick one
111: 
112: There is also a **layered** system — three shadows with increasing blur and decreasing opacity, mimicking how real light falls off:
113: 
114: ```css
115: box-shadow:
116:   0 1px 2px  rgba(17, 24, 39, .06),
117:   0 4px 8px  rgba(17, 24, 39, .04),
118:   0 12px 24px rgba(17, 24, 39, .03);
119: ```
120: 
121: That makes three systems in this skill: the **five-elevation** single shadow in `SKILL.md`, the **two-part** cast-plus-contact scale above, and this **layered** three-part set. They are parallel, not compatible, and mixing them in one project makes elevation unreadable — the same rule that applies between the first two.
122: 
123: Choose by how much work shadows do in the design. Five-elevation when they are incidental. Two-part when elevation is a real signal and press or drag states change it. Layered when the surface treatment is itself the design and the shadows are close to invisible individually.
124: 
125: ### Shadow color, and the pure-black question
126: 
127: The five-elevation scale uses `hsla(0,0%,0%,.2)` — pure black at low alpha. The layered system above deliberately does not, using a deep neutral (`rgba(17,24,39,…)`) instead, on the grounds that pure black reads harsh and artificial.
128: 
129: Both are right about different surfaces. Over a white or near-white page, black at low alpha resolves to a neutral grey and is indistinguishable from a tinted shadow. Over a **tinted, saturated or dark** surface it is not: black desaturates whatever it falls on, so the shadow reads as a grey smudge sitting on a colored ground rather than as an absence of light.
130: 
131: The rule: **tint the shadow toward the surface's own hue** — in practice, a dark step from the project's grey ramp rather than `hsl(0,0%,0%)` — whenever the surface under it is anything other than near-white. On a white page, keep the simpler black-alpha values.
132: 
133: The alpha difference between the two systems is not a disagreement. A single shadow carrying all the depth needs roughly `.2`; three stacked shadows each carry a fraction, which is why they sit near `.03` to `.06`. Do not port an alpha from one system into the other.
134: 
135: ### Animating a shadow
136: 
137: Transitioning `box-shadow` directly forces an expensive repaint on every frame. Put the target shadow on a pseudo-element and animate its `opacity` instead:
138: 
139: ```css
140: .card { position: relative; box-shadow: var(--shadow-1); }
141: .card::after {
142:   content: ''; position: absolute; inset: 0; border-radius: inherit;
143:   box-shadow: var(--shadow-3); opacity: 0; transition: opacity 180ms ease;
144:   pointer-events: none;
145: }
146: .card:hover::after { opacity: 1; }
147: ```
148: 
149: The duration belongs to the state-change band in [`motion-principles.md`](motion-principles.md) Section 5.
150: 
151: ### Full button anatomy
152: 
153: A button that reads as a physical object stacks six treatments rather than one shadow: an outer hairline cut that seats it into the surface, an inset ambient highlight on all sides, an inset top highlight for the light from above, at least three external depth shadows, a text drop-shadow for contrast against the fill, and a gradient so subtle that noticing it means it is too strong.
154: 
155: ```css
156: .button {
157:   background: linear-gradient(to bottom,
158:     color-mix(in srgb, var(--grey-900) 100%, white 4%), var(--grey-900));
159:   color: var(--grey-100);
160:   box-shadow:
161:     0 0 0 0.5px hsla(0,0%,0%,.3),               /* cut into the surface */
162:     inset 0 0 0 1px hsla(0,0%,100%,.04),        /* ambient highlight */
163:     inset 0 1px 0 hsla(0,0%,100%,.07),          /* light from above */
164:     0 1px 2px hsla(0,0%,0%,.1),
165:     0 2px 4px hsla(0,0%,0%,.06),
166:     0 4px 8px hsla(0,0%,0%,.03);
167:   text-shadow: 0 1px 1px hsla(0,0%,0%,.15);
168: }
169: ```
170: 
171: This is the layered system, so a project using it commits to layered elevation everywhere. It is worth the commitment only when buttons are a signature surface; a project where shadows are incidental should stay on the five-elevation scale and skip this entirely.
172: 
173: ---
174: 
175: ## 4. DEPTH WITHOUT SHADOWS
176: 
177: Flat design still conveys depth; it uses different cues.
178: 
179: - **Color.** Lighter feels closer, darker feels further away. A white card on a grey page pops forward; a grey well on a white page recedes.
180: - **Solid shadows.** A short vertical offset with **zero blur** — `0 3px 0 hsl(220,7%,83%)` — lifts a card off the page without breaking the flat aesthetic.
181: - **Overlap.** The strongest cue of all. Offset a card so it straddles the boundary between two background sections (`margin-bottom: -60px`), or make an element taller than its parent so it breaks out on both sides (`margin: -60px 0`). It works at component scale too: pull carousel arrows outside the slide with negative margins.
182: 
183: When overlapping images, give them a border in the **page background color** — an invisible border that guarantees a visual gap so the images never clash.
184: 
185: ---
186: 
187: ## 5. TYPOGRAPHY DETAIL
188: 
189: ### Baseline, not center
190: 
191: When two different font sizes sit on the same line — a card title and its "See all" action — vertical centering offsets their baselines and looks subtly wrong, especially when the sizes are close. Align to the baseline the eye is already reading from.
192: 
193: ```css
194: align-items: baseline;
195: ```
196: 
197: ### Letter-spacing
198: 
199: Default to trusting the type designer. There are two exceptions.
200: 
201: - **Headline use of a body typeface.** Faces built for legibility at small sizes have wider tracking than faces built for headlines. Tighten by about `-0.05em` to get that condensed headline feel. The reverse does not work — a headline face does not become legible at small sizes just because it was loosened.
202: - **All-caps.** Lowercase letters vary in shape through ascenders, descenders and x-height, which is what makes them scannable. Caps are uniform blocks, so default tracking crowds them. Add about `+0.05em`.
203: 
204: ### Line breaking
205: 
206: - **`text-wrap: balance` on headings.** Without it a headline commonly breaks into one long line and a short orphan. Balance evens the line lengths.
207: - **`text-wrap: pretty` on body text**, which reduces orphans without the cost of balancing every line.
208: - **Pair `text-align: justify` with `hyphens: auto`**, or do not justify. Justified text without hyphenation opens rivers of whitespace.
209: 
210: ### Underlines and synthesis
211: 
212: - **Offset underlines below descenders** so they read as intentional: `text-underline-offset: 3px` with `text-decoration-skip-ink: auto`. A default underline collides with every `g`, `p` and `y`.
213: - **`font-synthesis: none`** where a face lacks a real bold or italic. A browser-faked weight is a smeared outline, and it also breaks the two-weight rule by inventing a third.
214: - **Leave `font-optical-sizing: auto`** so variable faces adapt their glyphs to the rendered size.
215: 
216: ### Numerals
217: 
218: Use `font-variant-numeric: tabular-nums` wherever a digit change must not shift the layout: tables, dashboards, pricing, counters, timers. Use the default proportional figures in running prose, where tabular spacing looks mechanical.
219: 
220: For code-adjacent interfaces, a slashed zero removes the `0` versus `O` ambiguity, and a disambiguation stylistic set does the same for `I`, `l` and `1`.
221: 
222: ### Choosing typefaces without taste
223: 
224: - Neutral sans-serif is the safe default. The system font stack is a legitimate choice: `-apple-system, Segoe UI, Roboto, Noto Sans, Ubuntu, Cantarell, Helvetica Neue`.
225: - **Ignore families with fewer than five weights.** Filtering a font library to 10 or more styles cuts about 85% of the options, and what remains skews toward carefully-made families.
226: - Optimize for legibility: taller x-height, wider default tracking. Avoid condensed faces with short x-heights for UI text.
227: - Sort by popularity. A widely used font is usually a good font. Inspect sites worth admiring.
228: 
229: ---
230: 
231: ## 6. PERSONALITY IS FOUR DECISIONS
232: 
233: Personality is not a vibe. It is four concrete levers.
234: 
235: 1. **Typeface.** Serif reads elegant or classic. Rounded sans reads playful. Neutral sans reads plain and lets other elements carry the personality.
236: 2. **Color.** Blue is safe and nobody objects. Gold reads expensive. Pink reads fun.
237: 3. **Border radius.** Small is neutral, large is playful, none is formal. Be consistent.
238: 4. **Language.** "Thank you Mr. Benson" versus "Sweet, thanks Steve!" changes the product's character more than any color choice.
239: 
240: If the decision will not come, look at the other sites the users spend time in. Do not imitate direct competitors, or the result looks like a lesser version of them.
241: 
242: ---
243: 
244: ## 7. LAYOUT AND COMPONENT SHAPE
245: 
246: ### Grids are overrated
247: 
248: A grid is fluid percentage widths chosen from a constrained set. That is the wrong tool whenever an element has an optimal *fixed* size.
249: 
250: - **Sidebars** get a fixed width sized to their contents; the main area flexes and runs its own internal grid.
251: - **Cards and forms** get a `max-width` and shrink only when the viewport is actually smaller. Sizing a login card as "6 columns, then 8 columns at medium" produces the absurd result of the card being *wider* on medium screens than on large ones.
252: - Inside components, do not use a percentage unless the thing genuinely should scale.
253: 
254: Do not compromise a component's size until the screen actually forces it.
255: 
256: **Think in columns, not width.** When a component wants to stay narrow — a form field — but sits in a wide layout, do not stretch it to fill the space. Split the supporting content into its own column instead: a hint or error message beside the input rather than wrapped under it. That solves the "feels unbalanced" complaint without breaking the component's own sizing.
257: 
258: ### Concentric radius
259: 
260: When a rounded element sits inside another, the inner radius must equal the outer radius **minus the gap between them**. Giving both the same radius produces curves that visibly do not run parallel.
261: 
262: ```css
263: .outer {
264:   --padding: 8px;
265:   --inner-radius: 8px;
266:   border-radius: calc(var(--inner-radius) + var(--padding));
267:   padding: var(--padding);
268: }
269: .inner { border-radius: var(--inner-radius); }
270: ```
271: 
272: Deriving the outer radius from the inner one plus the padding keeps the relationship correct when either value changes.
273: 
274: ### Semi-transparent borders
275: 
276: A hardcoded border color is tuned to exactly one background. An alpha border adapts to whatever sits behind it, which matters for a component that appears on the page, in a well, and inside a modal.
277: 
278: This composes with the two border roles in `SKILL.md`: a decorative divider can be a low-alpha neutral, but a **functional** border still has to clear 3:1 against every background it will actually sit on. Alpha does not exempt it from the measurement; it just means the measurement has to be taken more than once.
279: 
280: ### Break the default component shape
281: 
282: Most components look generic because of an inherited mental picture, not a constraint.
283: 
284: - **Dropdown**: it is just a floating box. Give it sections, multiple columns, icons, descriptions under each item, a "NEW" badge.
285: - **Table**: columns do not have to hold one field each. Merge a non-sortable column into a related one — name over role, amount over policy type — to create hierarchy. Add avatars and colored status pills.
286: - **Radio group**: if the choice is central to the page, make them selectable cards showing the actual differences, not a stack of circles.
287: 
288: Constraints are powerful, but a design occasionally needs freedom from an assumption nobody checked.
289: 
290: ---
291: 
292: ## 8. WORKING WITH IMAGES
293: 
294: ### Text over photos
295: 
296: The problem is the image, not the text. Photos have bright and dark regions, so no single text color works everywhere. Reduce the image's dynamics:
297: 
298: - a semi-transparent overlay — `hsla(0,0%,0%,.55)` for light text, white for dark text
299: - lower the image's contrast, raising brightness to compensate; brightness `+40%` and contrast `-70%` is a reasonable start, then adjust by eye
300: - colorize: lower contrast, desaturate, then a solid fill in `multiply` blend mode
301: - a text-shadow used as a glow: large blur, no offset — `text-shadow: 0 0 50px hsla(0,0%,0%,.4)`
302: 
303: The glow preserves the most of the original photo.
304: 
305: ### Everything has an intended size
306: 
307: Icons drawn for 16 to 24px look chunky and detail-starved at 48px; icons drawn large look choppy when shrunk. If small icons are all that exists, put them at their real size inside a larger colored shape.
308: 
309: For screenshots, capture a smaller viewport, crop to one region, or draw a simplified illustration. Never shrink a full desktop screenshot by 70%. For favicons, redraw a simplified mark at the target size rather than letting the browser downscale the logo.
310: 
311: ### User-uploaded content
312: 
313: It cannot be controlled, so contain it.
314: 
315: - Fixed-size containers with `background-size: cover`, cropping the overflow.
316: - Prevent background bleed, where a user photo's edges match the UI background, with a subtle inset shadow — `box-shadow: inset 0 0 0 1px hsla(0,0%,0%,.1)` — rather than a border. Borders clash with the image's own colors; nobody notices the shadow.
317: 
318: ### Photos themselves
319: 
320: Bad photography ruins an otherwise good design. Hire a photographer or use good stock. Never design against placeholders while planning to shoot something on a phone later.
321: 
322: ---
323: 
324: ## 9. REFERENCES AND RELATED RESOURCES
325: 
326: - [`color-system.md`](color-system.md) — picking the `hsl()` values the lit edges and solid shadows above sample from.
327: - [`diagnosis-table.md`](diagnosis-table.md) Sections 5 and 6 — the typography and image symptoms these techniques fix.
328: - [`../assets/tokens.css`](../assets/tokens.css) — the five elevations as custom properties, plus the role layer these techniques sit on top of.

15: # Depth and Detail Techniques
16: 
17: The techniques that turn a correctly-scaled layout into something that looks finished: light, shadow, alignment, type detail, and images.
18: 
19: ---
20: 
21: ## 1. OVERVIEW
22: 
23: ### Core Principle
24: 
25: Borrow the real-world cue and stop. Depth comes from mimicking one light source consistently, not from chasing photorealism.
26: 
27: ### When to Use
28: 
29: - An element needs to read as raised, inset, or pressed.
30: - Shadows are prominent in the design and the five-elevation default is not enough.
31: - Typography looks subtly wrong at the detail level: mixed sizes on a line, all-caps labels, headline tracking.
32: - A component looks generic and nobody can say why.
33: - Images, screenshots, icons or user-uploaded content are breaking the layout.
34: 
35: ### Prerequisites
36: 
37: The default five-elevation shadow scale is in `SKILL.md` Section 3. Section 3 of this document gives the refined two-part alternative. The two are parallel systems — never mix them in one project.
38: 
39: ---
40: 
41: ## 2. EMULATING A LIGHT SOURCE
42: 
43: Raised and inset are the same trick: decide the element's **profile**, then mimic how light would hit that shape. Light comes from above, and people look slightly *down* at their screens, so the top edge of a raised element is visible and the bottom edge of an inset one is.
44: 
45: Each element needs **both** effects — the lit edge and the blocked light. They go in a single comma-separated `box-shadow`. Two `box-shadow` declarations on one selector do not combine; the second silently discards the first.
46: 
47: **Raised**, for a button or card: lit top edge, shadow cast below.
48: 
49: ```css
50: box-shadow:
51:   inset 0 1px 0 hsl(224, 84%, 74%),   /* top edge, angled toward the light */
52:   0 1px 3px hsla(0, 0%, 0%, .2);      /* light blocked beneath the element */
53: ```
54: 
55: **Inset**, for a well, text input or checkbox: lit bottom lip, shadow blocked at the top. The lip must be **lighter than the element's own face**, so the values depend entirely on how dark that face is.
56: 
57: ```css
58: /* Dark surface - the face is dark, so the lip has room to read as clearly lit. */
59: box-shadow:
60:   inset 0 -2px 0 hsl(211, 30%, 34%),    /* bottom lip, on a grey-800 face */
61:   inset 0 2px 2px hsla(0, 0%, 0%, .25); /* light blocked by the lip above */
62: 
63: /* Light surface - the face is already near-white, so there is almost no room to
64:    go lighter. Let the top shadow do the work and keep the lip to a hairline. */
65: box-shadow:
66:   inset 0 -1px 0 hsl(0, 0%, 100%),      /* on a grey-100 face */
67:   inset 0 2px 2px hsla(0, 0%, 0%, .06);
68: ```
69: 
70: Copying dark-surface values onto a white input paints a dark line along the bottom, which reads as a stray border — the opposite of the intended cue. Always check the lip against the face.
71: 
72: Both lit edges are `inset`. A non-inset shadow with a negative Y offset draws *above* the element, not on its bottom lip.
73: 
74: Two rules govern the lit edge:
75: 
76: - **Hand-pick the lighter color** rather than overlaying semi-transparent white. White overlays drain the saturation out of the underlying color, which is why both examples above use a solid `hsl()` sampled from the element's own hue. On a neutral grey or near-black surface there is no saturation to lose, so `hsla(0,0%,100%,.15)` is fine there.
77: - **Keep blur radii tiny.** These edges are sharp in the real world, like the shadow under a wall outlet.
78: 
79: ---
80: 
81: ## 3. TWO-PART SHADOWS
82: 
83: Good shadows are usually two shadows doing two different jobs.
84: 
85: - **Cast shadow**: larger and softer, bigger Y offset and blur. The shadow thrown behind the object by direct light.
86: - **Contact shadow**: tighter, small offset and blur. The area *underneath* the object that even ambient light cannot reach. This is what keeps the element's edges defined.
87: 
88: ```css
89: box-shadow:
90:   0 10px 20px hsla(0, 0%, 0%, .15),  /* cast    - larger, softer */
91:   0 3px 6px   hsla(0, 0%, 0%, .10);  /* contact - tighter, sharper */
92: ```
93: 
94: The two parts must differ *substantially* in offset and blur or the effect is invisible — about a threefold difference in both, as above.
95: 
96: **Which one is darker depends on elevation, and that is the whole point.** At rest on the surface the contact shadow is the darker of the two (`.24` against the cast shadow's `.12`). As the object lifts, the contact shadow fades out and ends up lighter, until at the top of the scale it is gone entirely. Do not fix the alphas; let them cross over. Keep both inside `.05` to `.25`, because anything heavier reads as a smudge.
97: 
98: ```css
99: /* lowest  */ 0 1px 3px hsla(0,0%,0%,.12), 0 1px 2px hsla(0,0%,0%,.24);
100: /*         */ 0 3px 6px hsla(0,0%,0%,.15), 0 2px 4px hsla(0,0%,0%,.12);
101: /*         */ 0 10px 20px hsla(0,0%,0%,.15), 0 3px 6px hsla(0,0%,0%,.10);
102: /*         */ 0 15px 25px hsla(0,0%,0%,.15), 0 5px 10px hsla(0,0%,0%,.05);
103: /* highest */ 0 20px 40px hsla(0,0%,0%,.2);
104: ```
105: 
106: Distinct at the lowest elevation, gone entirely at the highest — lift an object off a desk and the dark contact shadow disappears first.
107: 
108: The tradeoff: at the lowest elevations the two shadows converge in geometry (`0 1px 3px` plus `0 1px 2px`) and the technique buys little beyond a slightly crisper edge. That is why the plain five-elevation scale in `SKILL.md` remains the default when shadows are not prominent in the design.
109: 
110: ### Three parallel systems, pick one
111: 
112: There is also a **layered** system — three shadows with increasing blur and decreasing opacity, mimicking how real light falls off:
113: 
114: ```css
115: box-shadow:
116:   0 1px 2px  rgba(17, 24, 39, .06),
117:   0 4px 8px  rgba(17, 24, 39, .04),
118:   0 12px 24px rgba(17, 24, 39, .03);
119: ```
120: 
121: That makes three systems in this skill: the **five-elevation** single shadow in `SKILL.md`, the **two-part** cast-plus-contact scale above, and this **layered** three-part set. They are parallel, not compatible, and mixing them in one project makes elevation unreadable — the same rule that applies between the first two.
122: 
123: Choose by how much work shadows do in the design. Five-elevation when they are incidental. Two-part when elevation is a real signal and press or drag states change it. Layered when the surface treatment is itself the design and the shadows are close to invisible individually.
124: 
125: ### Shadow color, and the pure-black question
126: 
127: The five-elevation scale uses `hsla(0,0%,0%,.2)` — pure black at low alpha. The layered system above deliberately does not, using a deep neutral (`rgba(17,24,39,…)`) instead, on the grounds that pure black reads harsh and artificial.
128: 
129: Both are right about different surfaces. Over a white or near-white page, black at low alpha resolves to a neutral grey and is indistinguishable from a tinted shadow. Over a **tinted, saturated or dark** surface it is not: black desaturates whatever it falls on, so the shadow reads as a grey smudge sitting on a colored ground rather than as an absence of light.
130: 
131: The rule: **tint the shadow toward the surface's own hue** — in practice, a dark step from the project's grey ramp rather than `hsl(0,0%,0%)` — whenever the surface under it is anything other than near-white. On a white page, keep the simpler black-alpha values.
132: 
133: The alpha difference between the two systems is not a disagreement. A single shadow carrying all the depth needs roughly `.2`; three stacked shadows each carry a fraction, which is why they sit near `.03` to `.06`. Do not port an alpha from one system into the other.
134: 
135: ### Animating a shadow
136: 
137: Transitioning `box-shadow` directly forces an expensive repaint on every frame. Put the target shadow on a pseudo-element and animate its `opacity` instead:
138: 
139: ```css
140: .card { position: relative; box-shadow: var(--shadow-1); }
141: .card::after {
142:   content: ''; position: absolute; inset: 0; border-radius: inherit;
143:   box-shadow: var(--shadow-3); opacity: 0; transition: opacity 180ms ease;
144:   pointer-events: none;
145: }
146: .card:hover::after { opacity: 1; }
147: ```
148: 
149: The duration belongs to the state-change band in [`motion-principles.md`](motion-principles.md) Section 5.
150: 
151: ### Full button anatomy
152: 
153: A button that reads as a physical object stacks six treatments rather than one shadow: an outer hairline cut that seats it into the surface, an inset ambient highlight on all sides, an inset top highlight for the light from above, at least three external depth shadows, a text drop-shadow for contrast against the fill, and a gradient so subtle that noticing it means it is too strong.
154: 
155: ```css
156: .button {
157:   background: linear-gradient(to bottom,
158:     color-mix(in srgb, var(--grey-900) 100%, white 4%), var(--grey-900));
159:   color: var(--grey-100);
160:   box-shadow:
161:     0 0 0 0.5px hsla(0,0%,0%,.3),               /* cut into the surface */
162:     inset 0 0 0 1px hsla(0,0%,100%,.04),        /* ambient highlight */
163:     inset 0 1px 0 hsla(0,0%,100%,.07),          /* light from above */
164:     0 1px 2px hsla(0,0%,0%,.1),
165:     0 2px 4px hsla(0,0%,0%,.06),
166:     0 4px 8px hsla(0,0%,0%,.03);
167:   text-shadow: 0 1px 1px hsla(0,0%,0%,.15);
168: }
169: ```
170: 
171: This is the layered system, so a project using it commits to layered elevation everywhere. It is worth the commitment only when buttons are a signature surface; a project where shadows are incidental should stay on the five-elevation scale and skip this entirely.
172: 
173: ---
174: 
175: ## 4. DEPTH WITHOUT SHADOWS
176: 
177: Flat design still conveys depth; it uses different cues.
178: 
179: - **Color.** Lighter feels closer, darker feels further away. A white card on a grey page pops forward; a grey well on a white page recedes.
180: - **Solid shadows.** A short vertical offset with **zero blur** — `0 3px 0 hsl(220,7%,83%)` — lifts a card off the page without breaking the flat aesthetic.
181: - **Overlap.** The strongest cue of all. Offset a card so it straddles the boundary between two background sections (`margin-bottom: -60px`), or make an element taller than its parent so it breaks out on both sides (`margin: -60px 0`). It works at component scale too: pull carousel arrows outside the slide with negative margins.
182: 
183: When overlapping images, give them a border in the **page background color** — an invisible border that guarantees a visual gap so the images never clash.
184: 
185: ---
186: 
187: ## 5. TYPOGRAPHY DETAIL
188: 
189: ### Baseline, not center
190: 
191: When two different font sizes sit on the same line — a card title and its "See all" action — vertical centering offsets their baselines and looks subtly wrong, especially when the sizes are close. Align to the baseline the eye is already reading from.
192: 
193: ```css
194: align-items: baseline;
195: ```
196: 
197: ### Letter-spacing
198: 
199: Default to trusting the type designer. There are two exceptions.
200: 
201: - **Headline use of a body typeface.** Faces built for legibility at small sizes have wider tracking than faces built for headlines. Tighten by about `-0.05em` to get that condensed headline feel. The reverse does not work — a headline face does not become legible at small sizes just because it was loosened.
202: - **All-caps.** Lowercase letters vary in shape through ascenders, descenders and x-height, which is what makes them scannable. Caps are uniform blocks, so default tracking crowds them. Add about `+0.05em`.
203: 
204: ### Line breaking
205: 
206: - **`text-wrap: balance` on headings.** Without it a headline commonly breaks into one long line and a short orphan. Balance evens the line lengths.
207: - **`text-wrap: pretty` on body text**, which reduces orphans without the cost of balancing every line.
208: - **Pair `text-align: justify` with `hyphens: auto`**, or do not justify. Justified text without hyphenation opens rivers of whitespace.
209: 
210: ### Underlines and synthesis
211: 
212: - **Offset underlines below descenders** so they read as intentional: `text-underline-offset: 3px` with `text-decoration-skip-ink: auto`. A default underline collides with every `g`, `p` and `y`.
213: - **`font-synthesis: none`** where a face lacks a real bold or italic. A browser-faked weight is a smeared outline, and it also breaks the two-weight rule by inventing a third.
214: - **Leave `font-optical-sizing: auto`** so variable faces adapt their glyphs to the rendered size.
215: 
216: ### Numerals
217: 
218: Use `font-variant-numeric: tabular-nums` wherever a digit change must not shift the layout: tables, dashboards, pricing, counters, timers. Use the default proportional figures in running prose, where tabular spacing looks mechanical.
219: 
220: For code-adjacent interfaces, a slashed zero removes the `0` versus `O` ambiguity, and a disambiguation stylistic set does the same for `I`, `l` and `1`.
221: 
222: ### Choosing typefaces without taste
223: 
224: - Neutral sans-serif is the safe default. The system font stack is a legitimate choice: `-apple-system, Segoe UI, Roboto, Noto Sans, Ubuntu, Cantarell, Helvetica Neue`.
225: - **Ignore families with fewer than five weights.** Filtering a font library to 10 or more styles cuts about 85% of the options, and what remains skews toward carefully-made families.
226: - Optimize for legibility: taller x-height, wider default tracking. Avoid condensed faces with short x-heights for UI text.
227: - Sort by popularity. A widely used font is usually a good font. Inspect sites worth admiring.
228: 
229: ---
230: 
231: ## 6. PERSONALITY IS FOUR DECISIONS
232: 
233: Personality is not a vibe. It is four concrete levers.
234: 
235: 1. **Typeface.** Serif reads elegant or classic. Rounded sans reads playful. Neutral sans reads plain and lets other elements carry the personality.
236: 2. **Color.** Blue is safe and nobody objects. Gold reads expensive. Pink reads fun.
237: 3. **Border radius.** Small is neutral, large is playful, none is formal. Be consistent.
238: 4. **Language.** "Thank you Mr. Benson" versus "Sweet, thanks Steve!" changes the product's character more than any color choice.
239: 
240: If the decision will not come, look at the other sites the users spend time in. Do not imitate direct competitors, or the result looks like a lesser version of them.
241: 
242: ---
243: 
244: ## 7. LAYOUT AND COMPONENT SHAPE
245: 
246: ### Grids are overrated
247: 
248: A grid is fluid percentage widths chosen from a constrained set. That is the wrong tool whenever an element has an optimal *fixed* size.
249: 
250: - **Sidebars** get a fixed width sized to their contents; the main area flexes and runs its own internal grid.
251: - **Cards and forms** get a `max-width` and shrink only when the viewport is actually smaller. Sizing a login card as "6 columns, then 8 columns at medium" produces the absurd result of the card being *wider* on medium screens than on large ones.
252: - Inside components, do not use a percentage unless the thing genuinely should scale.
253: 
254: Do not compromise a component's size until the screen actually forces it.
255: 
256: **Think in columns, not width.** When a component wants to stay narrow — a form field — but sits in a wide layout, do not stretch it to fill the space. Split the supporting content into its own column instead: a hint or error message beside the input rather than wrapped under it. That solves the "feels unbalanced" complaint without breaking the component's own sizing.
257: 
258: ### Concentric radius
259: 
260: When a rounded element sits inside another, the inner radius must equal the outer radius **minus the gap between them**. Giving both the same radius produces curves that visibly do not run parallel.
261: 
262: ```css
263: .outer {
264:   --padding: 8px;
265:   --inner-radius: 8px;
266:   border-radius: calc(var(--inner-radius) + var(--padding));
267:   padding: var(--padding);
268: }
269: .inner { border-radius: var(--inner-radius); }
270: ```
271: 
272: Deriving the outer radius from the inner one plus the padding keeps the relationship correct when either value changes.
273: 
274: ### Semi-transparent borders
275: 
276: A hardcoded border color is tuned to exactly one background. An alpha border adapts to whatever sits behind it, which matters for a component that appears on the page, in a well, and inside a modal.
277: 
278: This composes with the two border roles in `SKILL.md`: a decorative divider can be a low-alpha neutral, but a **functional** border still has to clear 3:1 against every background it will actually sit on. Alpha does not exempt it from the measurement; it just means the measurement has to be taken more than once.
279: 
280: ### Break the default component shape
281: 
282: Most components look generic because of an inherited mental picture, not a constraint.
283: 
284: - **Dropdown**: it is just a floating box. Give it sections, multiple columns, icons, descriptions under each item, a "NEW" badge.
285: - **Table**: columns do not have to hold one field each. Merge a non-sortable column into a related one — name over role, amount over policy type — to create hierarchy. Add avatars and colored status pills.
286: - **Radio group**: if the choice is central to the page, make them selectable cards showing the actual differences, not a stack of circles.
287: 
288: Constraints are powerful, but a design occasionally needs freedom from an assumption nobody checked.
289: 
290: ---
291: 
292: ## 8. WORKING WITH IMAGES
293: 
294: ### Text over photos
295: 
296: The problem is the image, not the text. Photos have bright and dark regions, so no single text color works everywhere. Reduce the image's dynamics:
297: 
298: - a semi-transparent overlay — `hsla(0,0%,0%,.55)` for light text, white for dark text
299: - lower the image's contrast, raising brightness to compensate; brightness `+40%` and contrast `-70%` is a reasonable start, then adjust by eye
300: - colorize: lower contrast, desaturate, then a solid fill in `multiply` blend mode
301: - a text-shadow used as a glow: large blur, no offset — `text-shadow: 0 0 50px hsla(0,0%,0%,.4)`
302: 
303: The glow preserves the most of the original photo.
304: 
305: ### Everything has an intended size
306: 
307: Icons drawn for 16 to 24px look chunky and detail-starved at 48px; icons drawn large look choppy when shrunk. If small icons are all that exists, put them at their real size inside a larger colored shape.
308: 
309: For screenshots, capture a smaller viewport, crop to one region, or draw a simplified illustration. Never shrink a full desktop screenshot by 70%. For favicons, redraw a simplified mark at the target size rather than letting the browser downscale the logo.
310: 
311: ### User-uploaded content
312: 
313: It cannot be controlled, so contain it.
314: 
315: - Fixed-size containers with `background-size: cover`, cropping the overflow.
316: - Prevent background bleed, where a user photo's edges match the UI background, with a subtle inset shadow — `box-shadow: inset 0 0 0 1px hsla(0,0%,0%,.1)` — rather than a border. Borders clash with the image's own colors; nobody notices the shadow.
317: 
318: ### Photos themselves
319: 
320: Bad photography ruins an otherwise good design. Hire a photographer or use good stock. Never design against placeholders while planning to shoot something on a phone later.
321: 
322: ---
323: 
324: ## 9. REFERENCES AND RELATED RESOURCES
325: 
326: - [`color-system.md`](color-system.md) — picking the `hsl()` values the lit edges and solid shadows above sample from.
327: - [`diagnosis-table.md`](diagnosis-table.md) Sections 5 and 6 — the typography and image symptoms these techniques fix.
328: - [`../assets/tokens.css`](../assets/tokens.css) — the five elevations as custom properties, plus the role layer these techniques sit on top of.

15: # Building the Color System
16: 
17: The scales in `SKILL.md` say *what* to define. This says how to pick the values, and how to keep them from looking washed out or failing contrast.
18: 
19: ---
20: 
21: ## 1. OVERVIEW
22: 
23: ### Core Principle
24: 
25: A palette is built once, from the edges inward, and adjusted by eye. The moment new shades get added outside the system, there is no system.
26: 
27: ### When to Use
28: 
29: - Designing a palette or token set from scratch.
30: - Extending an existing ramp to a new accent or to dark mode.
31: - A color fails contrast and raising lightness is making it worse.
32: - Greys look flat, or the palest and darkest shades have drifted toward neutral.
33: 
34: ### Prerequisites
35: 
36: The shade-count and naming rules — 8 to 10 greys, 5 to 10 shades per primary and accent, named `100` through `900` with base `500` — are in `SKILL.md` Section 3. This document assumes them.
37: 
38: ---
39: 
40: ## 2. WHY HSL
41: 
42: Hex and RGB describe colors in terms a machine cares about. HSL describes them in the terms the eye already uses.
43: 
44: - **Hue** is position on the wheel, in degrees: 0 red, 120 green, 240 blue. This is what makes two different colors both read as "blue".
45: - **Saturation** is how vivid. 0% is grey, at which point hue is meaningless; 100% is intense.
46: - **Lightness** is 0% black, 100% white, 50% the pure hue.
47: 
48: Two shades of the same color share a hue in HSL and look nothing alike in hex.
49: 
50: Design tools mostly show HSB and browsers only understand HSL, so do not confuse them. In HSB, 100% brightness is only white when saturation is 0; HSB at S100/B100 equals HSL at S100/L50.
51: 
52: ---
53: 
54: ## 3. BUILDING THE RAMP
55: 
56: ### Picking the base (500)
57: 
58: There is no formula. For a primary or accent color, pick the shade that **works as a button background** — dark enough that white text sits on it comfortably, light enough that the button does not read as black. Rules such as "start at 50% lightness" do not hold, because every hue behaves differently. Use your eyes.
59: 
60: For greys the base matters less. Work from the edges instead: the darkest grey is whatever the darkest text should be, and the lightest is a subtle off-white background.
61: 
62: ### Finding the edges (900 and 100)
63: 
64: Choose them by imagining where they will be used. `900` is almost always a text color and `100` is almost always a background tint. A simple alert component uses both at once — dark text on a pale tinted panel — so design one and read both values off it.
65: 
66: ### Filling the gaps
67: 
68: With `900`, `500` and `100` fixed, add `700` and `300` as the perfect compromise between the shades on either side. That leaves four holes — `800`, `600`, `400`, `200` — filled the same way. Nine shades is convenient because it divides cleanly.
69: 
70: Then adjust by eye. A systematic build gets 90% of the way there; expect to nudge a saturation or push a shade lighter once it is in use.
71: 
72: What must *not* happen is new shades appearing outside the system when something does not quite fit. That is the failure this whole method exists to prevent.
73: 
74: ---
75: 
76: ## 4. KEEPING SATURATION ALIVE
77: 
78: In HSL, saturation's effect weakens as lightness approaches 0% or 100%. The same S value that looks vivid at L50 looks washed out at L90.
79: 
80: **So: increase saturation as lightness moves away from 50%, in both directions.** The lightest and darkest shades should carry *more* saturation than the base, not the same amount. The difference is subtle per swatch and very visible once the color covers a large area.
81: 
82: This applies to greys too. Tinted greys without raised saturation at the ends will drift back toward neutral at the palest and darkest steps.
83: 
84: ---
85: 
86: ## 5. PERCEIVED BRIGHTNESS AND HUE ROTATION
87: 
88: Every hue has an inherent perceived brightness. Yellow and blue at identical HSL lightness look nothing alike, because the eye weights the channels unevenly:
89: 
90: ```text
91: perceived brightness = sqrt(0.299·r² + 0.587·g² + 0.114·b²) / 255
92: ```
93: 
94: Across the wheel this gives three local maxima — **60° yellow, 180° cyan, 300° magenta** — and three minima — **0° red, 120° green, 240° blue**.
95: 
96: That is a second way to change how light a color looks, without touching lightness and without draining its intensity:
97: 
98: - **To lighten:** rotate the hue toward the nearest of 60°, 180° or 300°.
99: - **To darken:** rotate the hue toward the nearest of 0°, 120° or 240°.
100: 
101: **Cap the rotation at 20 to 30 degrees total.** Beyond that it reads as a different color rather than a lighter or darker one.
102: 
103: This is the fix for scales built on light hues. A yellow darkened by lightness alone goes muddy olive-brown; a yellow darkened by rotating gradually toward orange gives warm, rich dark shades. Combine both approaches freely — take some brightness from hue and some from lightness.
104: 
105: ### Warm and cool greys
106: 
107: True grey is S0%, no color at all. Most greys in good UIs are saturated noticeably.
108: 
109: - **Cool**, blue-ish: hue about 207 to 210, saturation about 12 to 21%.
110: - **Warm**, yellow or orange-ish: hue about 39 to 41, saturation about 12 to 21%.
111: 
112: How far to push it is a personality decision. The saturation rule in Section 4 still applies: raise S at the light and dark ends or the extremes will look flat next to the mid-tones.
113: 
114: ---
115: 
116: ## 6. HITTING CONTRAST RATIOS WITHOUT UGLY COLOR
117:

24:

35:

37: 
38: ---
39: 
40: ## 2. WHY HSL
41: 
42: Hex and RGB describe colors in terms a machine cares about. HSL describes them in the terms the eye already uses.
43: 
44: - **Hue** is position on the wheel, in degrees: 0 red, 120 green, 240 blue. This is what makes two different colors both read as "blue".
45: - **Saturation** is how vivid. 0% is grey, at which point hue is meaningless; 100% is intense.
46: - **Lightness** is 0% black, 100% white, 50% the pure hue.
47: 
48: Two shades of the same color share a hue in HSL and look nothing alike in hex.
49: 
50: Design tools mostly show HSB and browsers only understand HSL, so do not confuse them. In HSB, 100% brightness is only white when saturation is 0; HSB at S100/B100 equals HSL at S100/L50.

52: ---
53:

55: 
56: ### Picking the base (500)
57: 
58: There is no formula. 59:

73:
